questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient sustained a fracture as depicted in the image, following a fall from height. What is this fracture known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Open book fracture

The fracture shown in the image is known as Open book fracture.

Open book fractures are associated with pubic diastasis and/or a fracture of the pubic rami with a posterior pelvic disruption of the sacro-iliac joint.

Other options:

Malgaigne's fracture(image shown below)  involves the pubic rami anteriorly and the sacroiliac joint (SI joint) or ilium near the SI joint on the same side posteriorly.

Bucket handle fracture refers to a vertically orientated fracture through ipsilateral superior and inferior pubic rami with contralateral sacroiliac joint disruption.

Chauffeur's fracture refers to fracture of the radial styloid process in the forearm.
questions.learning: Open book fracture — The fracture shown in the image is known as Open book fracture. Open book fractures are associated with pubic diastasis and/or a fracture of the pubic rami with a posterior pelvic disruption of the sacro-iliac joint.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) suggesting imminent necrosis is indicated by which of the following values? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. <0.3

The Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is a quantitative assessment tool that measures the ratio of systolic blood pressure at the ankle to that in the ipsilateral arm. The normal resting ABPI ranges from 0.9-1.3. As ABPI decreases, it indicates progressively worsening arterial obstruction. An ABPI value of <0.3 specifically indicates imminent necrosis - the most severe stage of arterial insufficiency, where tissue death is about to occur.

questions.text: The common carotid artery pulse is assessed at the level of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cricoid cartilage

The common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

The common carotid artery pulse is assessed at the level of the neck, typically just lateral to the trachea, where the artery can be palpated against the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Position the fingers between the larynx and the front edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of the cricoid cartilage. When palpating the pulse, adjust the pressure on the artery until the strongest pulsation is felt.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the standard normal distribution curve is true?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mean = Median

The standard normal distribution (also called Gaussian distribution) is a perfectly symmetrical, bell-shaped curve. Its properties :

Key properties:

| Property | Value

| -------- | -----

| Shape | Perfectly symmetrical, bell-shaped

| Mean | = Median = Mode

| Skewness | Zero (no skew)

| Total area under curve | = 1 (or 100%)

| Mean ± 1 SD | Covers 68.27% of observations

| Mean ± 2 SD | Covers 95.45% of observations

| Mean ± 3 SD | Covers 99.73% of observations

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 11-14 weeks

The best time to determine chorionicity and amnionicity in twin pregnancy is during the first trimester, especially between 11–14 weeks of gestation.

Why this period is ideal:

• Membranes and placental relationships are clearly visible
• Lambda (twin peak) sign and T-sign can be identified accurately
• Early diagnosis guides antenatal surveillance and management

Ultrasound findings:

• Lambda (twin peak) sign → dichorionic twins
• T-sign → monochorionic twins

Importance of determining chorionicity:

• Monochorionic twins have higher risks of:

• Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)
• Selective fetal growth restriction
• Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence
• Increased perinatal morbidity and mortality

Accuracy of chorionicity assessment decreases later in pregnancy as membranes become thinner and placentas may fuse.
questions.learning: 11-14 weeks The best time to determine chorionicity and amnionicity in twin pregnancy is during the first trimester, especially between 11–14 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Most common genetic cause of hypercoagulability is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Factor V Leiden mutation

The most common genetic cause of hypercoagulability is the Factor V Leiden mutation.

Primary (inherited) hypercoagulability is most often caused by mutations in the factor V and prothrombin genes. Factor V Leiden mutation is the most common cause followed by prothrombin G20210A mutation.

The Leiden mutation is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The mutation makes factor V resistant to cleavage and inactivation by protein C. This leads to the inactivation of an important antithrombotic counterregulatory pathway.

Protein C, Protein S, and antithrombin III deficiency are rare causes of primary hypercoagulability.

Other options:

Option B: Protein C deficiency causes thrombosis in teenagers. It may also be induced by liver dysfunction, vitamin K antagonists, renal failure, DIC, and active thrombosis.

Option C: Antithrombin III forms a complex with thrombin by binding to heparin on endothelial cells. This complex inhibits coagulation. Its deficiency presents as early-age thrombosis (less than 50 years old) and it carries the highest risk for thrombotic events among the inherited thrombophilias.

Option D: The prothrombin G20210A mutation results in increased levels of prothrombin which demonstrates a higher risk for arterial and venous thrombotic events.
questions.learning: Factor V Leiden mutation — The most common genetic cause of hypercoagulability is the Factor V Leiden mutation. Primary (inherited) hypercoagulability is most often caused by mutations in the factor V and prothrombin genes.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Arsenic poisoning may mimic all of the following conditions except:
options: Addison’s disease due to hyperpigmentation and GI disturbances
Guillain-Barré syndrome due to ascending peripheral neuropathy
Diabetes insipidus due to renal concentrating defects
Korsakoff’s syndrome due to neurocognitive impairment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diabetes insipidus due to renal concentrating defects

• Arsenic poisoning can mimic several medical conditions due to its multisystem effects.
• It causes hyperpigmentation, GI symptoms, and hypotension, resembling Addison’s disease.
• It can produce ascending peripheral neuropathy, clinically similar to Guillain–Barré syndrome, and chronic exposure may lead to neurocognitive impairment, mimicking Korsakoff’s syndrome.
• However, arsenic does not cause diabetes insipidus, as it does not produce a primary defect in ADH secretion or renal concentrating ability.
• Hence, this condition is not mimicked by arsenic poisoning.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of thiazides in DCT?
options: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule
Inhibits the Na-CI pump in late distal convoluted tubule
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the descending limb of loop of Henle
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule

Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the Na+/Cl- co-transporter.

Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits the Na Cl symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride.

Thiazide diuretics:

They may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the NaCl co-transporter in the DCT. This results in the loss of sodium, chloride, and water contributing to the diuretic effect. The diuretic effect of thiazide leads to decreased osmotic pressure due to the loss of Na+, Cl-, and water leading to compensatory reabsorption of uric acid thus resulting in hyperuricemia. The intracytoplasmic Na+ concentration also decreases due to the blockade of the co-transporter. To compensate, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger pumps sodium from the systemic circulation into the epithelial cells in exchange for calcium. The declining calcium levels inside the cell will draw more calcium from the lumen into the systemic circulation. This results in hypercalcemia. There is also increased loss of Mg2+, K+, and H+.

Mechanisms of antihypertensive action: Decreases plasma and ECF volume by diuresis thereby decreasing cardiac output. Even when the compensatory mechanisms restore the Na+ levels and plasma volume, a low BP is maintained by a reduction in total peripheral resistance. This reduction in total peripheral resistance is due to the persistence of a small sodium and volume deficit even after compensation. The decreased intracellular sodium is responsible for increased compliance of the vessel wall and a reduced response to constrictor stimulus.

Thiazides are the diuretic of choice for uncomplicated hypertension.

Advantages of thiazide as an antihypertensive are:

* It can be given as once a day dose and has a flat dose-response curve

* Decreased incidence of postural hypotension and relative freedom from CNS side effects

* No tolerance

* No fluid retention

* Decreased risk of osteoporotic fractures due to its hypocalciuric action

* Low cost

* Effectiveness in isolated systolic hypertension

* Thiazides are ineffective both as antihypertensive and diuretic in patients with chronic renal failure.
questions.learning: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the Na+/Cl- co-transporter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old patient with a known history of lung cancer presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath. On physical examination, bronchial breath sounds and a dull note on percussion are detected in the left infrascapular area. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of lung cancer and increasing dyspnea suggests a common complication like fluid accumulation. The clinical findings of a dull percussion note and bronchial breathing (which occurs just above the fluid level) in the left base are hallmark signs of a Pleural Effusion. The provided chest X-ray provides definitive radiological confirmation, showing a homogenous opacification of the left lung base with a classic meniscus sign (concave upper border). Cardiac tamponade (Option A) and pericarditis (Option B) would present with heart-specific signs like muffled sounds and JVP changes. Pulmonary embolism (Option C) typically presents with a normal chest X-ray or non-specific wedge shadows. Therefore, given the specific combination of lung malignancy, pathognomonic physical signs, and clear radiographic meniscus, a left-sided pleural effusion is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A G2P1L1 woman with a previous history of breech delivery underwent an LSCS which was uneventful. Now, she was brought to the ER with an antepartum haemorrhage and was shifted for LSCS during which she lost a lot of blood. An obstetric hysterectomy had to be carried out. An image of the uterus is given below. What is the diagnosis?

LSCS - lower segment cesearean section
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placenta accreta syndrome

The given clinical scenario of this woman with previous LSCS, bleeding per vaginum during pregnancy with hysterectomy image showing placenta adherent to the uterine wall suggests that it is a case of placenta accreta syndrome.

Placenta accreta is described as an abnormally implanted, invasive, or adhered placenta. It is due to the partial or total absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the Nitabuch layer.

Nitabuch layer is a layer of fibrin between the compact endometrium and the cytotrophoblastic shell in the placenta. This layer is absent in the placenta accreta.

There are 3 variants of placenta accreta syndrome. They are :

• Placenta accreta - villi are attached to the myometrium.
• Placenta increta - villi invade the myometrium.
• Placenta percreta - villi penetrate through the myometrium and to or through the serosa.
questions.learning: Placenta accreta syndrome — The given clinical scenario of this woman with previous LSCS, bleeding per vaginum during pregnancy with hysterectomy image showing placenta adherent to the uterine wall suggests that it is a case of placenta accreta syndrome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is given to prevent neural tube defects in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folic Acid

Folic acid (Vitamin B9) is given to prevent the incidence of neural tube defects.

Folic acid deficiency is implicated in neural tube defects like spina bifida, encephalocele, and anencephaly.

* Supplementation of folic acid, in doses of 400 μg/day, prior to conception has been shown to cause a significant reduction in the incidence of spina bifida and other neural tube defects.

* Reduced activity of the enzyme 5,10-methylene-THF reductase (MTHFR) caused by a common C677T polymorphism in the MTHFR gene is one of the causes of Neural tube defects in Folate deficiency.

As per the Anemia Mukt Bharat Program, during the period of pre-conception up to the first trimester, women are advised to have 400 mcg of folic acid tablets daily to reduce the incidence of neural tube defects in the fetus.

Note that, non-pregnant, non-lactating women of reproductive age (20–49 years) who are not actively planning a pregnancy in the near term should receive 1 iron and folic acid tablet containing 60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is Prosopagnosia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Difficulty in identifying known faces

Prosopagnosia is difficulty in identifying known faces.

In humans, storage and recognition of faces is more strongly represented in the right inferior temporal lobe in right-handed individuals, though the left lobe is also active. Damage to this area can cause prosopagnosia.

Patients with this abnormality can recognize forms and reproduce them. They can recognize people by their voices, and many of them show autonomic responses when they see familiar as opposed to unfamiliar faces. However, they cannot identify the familiar faces they see. The left hemisphere is also involved, but the role of the right hemisphere is primary.

The presence of autonomic response to a familiar face in the absence of recognition has been explained by postulating the existence of a separate dorsal pathway for processing information about faces that leads to recognition at only a subconscious level.

Note:

• Autotopagnosia - inability to recognize or to orient any part of one's own body
• Simultagnosia - inability to recognize multiple elements in a visual presentation, one object or some elements of a scene can be appreciated but not the display as a whole
• Somatagnosia - inability to identify any part of the body, either one’s own or another’s body
• Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) -  inability to recognize objects by touch, in the presence of intact cutaneous and proprioceptive hand sensation; caused by a lesion in the contralateral parietal lobe

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient with a history of schizophrenia, and on treatment for drug-induced Parkinson's presents with complaints of constipation, blurred vision, and dry mouth. Which of the following drugs may be responsible for the above symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benzhexol

This patient with schizophrenia and drug-induced parkinson's disease with anti-cholinergic symptoms is taking benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl).

Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a condition that is caused by certain drugs that have D2 antagonistic action like typical antipsychotics. Due to the decrease in dopaminergic activity, they result in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Benzhexol is a centrally-acting antimuscarinic agent. It acts by restoring the cholinergic balance in the striatal interneurons.

The following drugs are implicated in drug-induced parkinsonism:

Drug class

Examples

Typical antipsychotics

Phenothiazines, haloperidol

Atypical antipsychotics
Risperidone, olanzapine

Dopamine depleters
Reserpine, tetrabenazine

Antiemetics
Metoclopramide, levosulpiride

Calcium channel blockers
Flunarizine, cinnarizine

Other options:

Option A: Lithium is used to treat bipolar disorders and major depressive disorder. The main adverse effects are lithium toxicity, serotonin syndrome, and pseudotumor cerebri. Lithium use is usually avoided in patients with a known cardiovascular disease due to an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias.

Option B: Pramipexole is used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease and restless leg syndrome. The main adverse effects are dyskinesias and postural deformities.

Option D: Selegiline is used in the treatment of major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease. The main adverse effects are serotonin syndrome, somnolence, and exacerbation of hypertension. Hence, it is not preferred in Parkinson's patients with hypertension.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: There is an intracellular buildup of cholesterol and cholesterol esters/fats in all of the following conditions except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abetalipoproteinemia

Abetalipoproteinemia is a rare genetic disorder in which there is defective chylomicron formation leading to low plasma lipids and no intracellular cholesterol accumulation.

Chylomicrons are required for the absorption and transport of fats and fat-soluble vitamins. It presents in early childhood with steatorrhoea, hypolipidemia, failure to thrive, ataxia, sensory and motor neuropathies.

Abetalipoproteinemia is a rare autosomal recessive disease, caused due to the mutation in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP). MTTP is necessary to transfer lipids to the small intestine's nascent chylomicrons and Very Low-Density Lipoprotein (VLDL)  in the liver. In abetalipoproteinemia, there is an absence of chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL (apoB containing lipoproteins), and deficient levels of plasma cholesterol and triglycerides.

Other options:

Option A) Tendon xanthomas: Tendon xanthomas appear as nodules or plaques within tendons caused by the buildup of cholesterol and its esters. They are typically linked to lipid metabolism disorders. Familial hypercholesterolemia is the most common associated condition.

Option C) Strawberry gallbladder: Strawberry gallbladder, also termed cholesterolosis, refers to the deposition of cholesterol within the mucosa of the gallbladder, resulting in a strawberry-like appearance.

Option D) Niemann-Pick disease: occurs due to the deficient activity of acid sphingomyelinase enzyme. There is extensive accumulation of sphingomyelin in the monocyte-macrophage system. Lipid-laden foam cells are observed in bone marrow and lymph nodes. In Niemann Pick Type C, there is accumulation of cholesterol in lysosomes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Five days after a common bile duct injury, there is a leak, and the patient presents with fever and abdominal pain . What will be the next line of management ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ultrasound-guided aspiration

In the case of a common bile duct injury with a leak and patient presenting with signs of localized peritonitis, the next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by ERCP and stenting.

Common bile duct injury: The most common cause of bile duct injury is laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Management

* If detected on table with

* Duct injury less than 3 mm or those draining less than single segment of the liver: Ligation

* Lateral injury—Duct injury more than 4 mm or those draining multiple hepatic segments: Repair using T-tube.

* Transection with minimal loss of duct length: Repair using T-tube is used; in case of extensive loss of duct length, billiary enteric anastomosis is performed.

* Cystic duct leaks can be treated by the percutaneous drainage of intra-abdominal collection and endoscopic biliary drainage.

* Post-operative detection of leak: Major biliary leakage is usually seen 2 to 10 days after cholecystectomy. Patients usually present with pain in the abdominal region, fever, and, in some cases, bilious ascitic fluid.

* Jaundice is usually mild. Leukocytosis and abnormal liver function tests, particularly elevations in the serum levels of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, are common.

* Radiological workup: Upon presentation, transabdominal ultrasonography is initially performed to define the extent of possible bile leak.

* For definitive leaks, ultrasound-guided aspiration is performed; alternatively, the collection is drained and a transhepatic biliary drain is placed. After 6–8 weeks, the definitive repair is ascertained.

* Ultrasonography confirmation and aspiration of the leak is followed by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and stenting.
questions.learning: Ultrasound-guided aspiration — In the case of a common bile duct injury with a leak and patient presenting with signs of localized peritonitis, the next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by ERCP and stenting.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came to casualty complaining of a severe headache. On examination, there was no focal neurological defect. However, neck rigidity was present. The casualty medical officer ordered an emergency CT which revealed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH).

The most common cause of SAH is trauma. The most common spontaneous cause of SAH is the rupture of berry aneurysms.

It clinically presents as a thunderclap headache with neck rigidity, transient loss of consciousness and no focal neurological deficit. Non-contrast CT shows blood in the basal cistern.

Although sudden headache in the absence of focal neurological symptoms is the hallmark of aneurysmal rupture, focal neurological deficits may occur.

Pearl PF0339: Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH)

* Source: Arterial bleed

* MC- Middle meningeal artery

* Cause- Trauma

* Clinical features: Lucid interval is characteristic

* CT – Lentiform opacity

* Treatment: A large or rapidly evolving EDH requires surgical evacuation

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous bleed

* Bridging dural veins

* Causes: Trauma, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol abuse, shaken baby syndrome

* Clinical features

* Acute SDH: may be associated with lucid interval

* Chronic SDH: drowsiness, headache

* CT- crescentic opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

* Source: Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – Trauma

* 2nd MC – Rupture of berry aneurysm

* MC sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness +/- FND

* Investigations:

* Non-contrast CT brain,

* CSF xanthochromia (peaks in 2 days and subsides in 2 weeks)

* Treatment:

* Clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm,

* Triple H therapy – hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution to prevent vasospasm

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage- (MC type of ICH)

* Source- Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – hypertension

* Trauma, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, bleeding disorders, neoplasms, vascular malformations

* MC sites:

* Putamen (basal ganglia)

* Thalamus

* Cerebellum

* Pons

* Treatment:

* Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP or fresh platelets as required

* Surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoms >3 cm in size

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with uterine inversion is taken for laparotomy after failed manual methods. On traction on the round ligaments, the inverted fundus begins to rise through the cervical ring and the uterus is restored without incising the ring. What is the indicated operative method called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Huntington method

In uterine inversion refractory to manual replacement, operative correction can be performed at laparotomy. If the surgeon applies upward traction on the round ligaments or the inverted uterine fundus using clamps, gradually “walking” the uterus back through the cervical ring without incising the constriction ring, this is the Huntington procedure. The stem explicitly states that the uterus is restored without incising the ring, which distinguishes Huntington from Haultain.

● Huntington method: laparotomy, identify the cup-shaped inversion, apply traction on round ligaments or fundus, progressively elevating the uterus through the ring without cutting the ring.

●  Haultain method: used when the cervical ring is tight and replacement fails. It involves posterior incision of the constriction ring to allow reposition.

Other options:

B. Haultain method

Incorrect here because Haultain requires incision of the constriction ring (usually posterior). The stem states no incision was needed.

C. B-Lynch suture

Used for uterine atony causing postpartum hemorrhage as a uterine compression suture, not for inversion reduction.

D. Hayman suture

Another uterine compression suture for atonic postpartum hemorrhage, not a method for inversion correction.

Huntington procedure:

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Among the drugs used for the acute management of asthma, which one does not act by causing bronchodilation?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone is a systemic corticosteroid that acts primarily by suppressing the underlying inflammatory response rather than through direct bronchodilation. It reduces airway mucosal edema and decreases the production of inflammatory mediators over several hours. Salbutamol (Option A) is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that directly relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, providing rapid widening of the airways. Ipratropium (Option B) is an anticholinergic agent that blocks muscarinic receptors, thereby preventing bronchoconstriction. Deriphyllin (Option C), a combination containing theophylline derivatives, works by inhibiting phosphodiesterase and antagonizing adenosine receptors to cause bronchodilation. While hydrocortisone is essential in managing an acute asthma exacerbation to prevent late-phase reactions and reduce the need for hospitalization, it does not provide the immediate relief of airway obstruction seen with the other listed bronchodilators. Corticosteroids are delayed-onset life-savers in asthma management, whereas beta-agonists are the immediate relievers
questions.learning: Hydrocortisone is a systemic corticosteroid that acts primarily by suppressing the underlying inflammatory response rather than through direct bronchodilation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pre-menopausal woman is diagnosed with lymph node-positive, early invasive breast cancer. IHC reveals ER +, PR +, and HER-2-neu 1+. Which of the following drug will you provide for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tamoxifen

The given clinical scenario suggests early invasive breast cancer in a pre-menopausal woman, which is lymph node-positive, hormone receptor-positive (ER/PR +), and Her-2/neu negative (Her-2/neu IHC score of 1+ is considered negative). Hence Tamoxifen is the drug of choice.

Treatment of early-stage breast cancer (T1-2 N0-1 M0) includes:

Breast conservation surgery (BCS) + ALND or SLNB + Radiotherapy

• BCS is followed by radiotherapy
• Mastectomy is done if BCS is contraindicated.
• Clinical N0 status-sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) at the time of surgery.
• Clinical N1 status-ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA): axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) if positive and sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) if negative.

Endocrine therapy: for hormone receptor (ER/PR) positive

• For Premenopausal women-tamoxifen (selective estrogen receptor modulator, SERM)
• For post-menopausal women (usually >50 years)-anastrozole (Aromatase inhibitor)
• Tamoxifen has an agonistic action on the endometrium, leading to an increased risk of endometrial cancers Hence, it is not used in post-menopausal women.

Anti-Her-2 therapy: for Her-2/neu positive breast cancer

• Trastuzumab is given
• Her-2/neu IHC interpretation:

•   0 or 1+ = Negative
•   2+ = Equivocal cases ->        confirmed with Fluorescence    in situ hybridization (FISH)      analysis
•   3+ = Positive

Chemotherapy

Indicated for:

• Lymph nodes positive
• Lymph nodes negative but tumor size of >1 cm
• Lymph nodes negative and tumor size of >0.5 cm with

• Blood vessel/Lymph vessel invasion
• ER/PR –ve
• Her-2/neu overexpression
• High grade

• Triple-negative breast carcinoma
• High recurrence score after Oncotype Dx

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The risk of fetal varicella syndrome is maximum when the mother is infected between _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 13 to 20 weeks

The risk of developing fetal varicella syndrome (congenital varicella syndrome) is highest when the mother develops varicella infection between 13 to 20 weeks.

Congenital varicella syndrome occurs in 2% of infants with maternal varicella between 13 and 20 weeks of gestation and in 0.4% of infants before 13 weeks of gestation. It is rare after 20 weeks.

Congenital varicella syndrome is characterized by cicatricial skin scarring in a zoster-like pattern (zig-zag scarring), and limb hypoplasia (shown below). They can also present with neurological abnormalities (microcephaly, cortical atrophy, mental retardation), ophthalmic features (chorioretinitis, microphthalmia, cataract), and renal and autonomic system abnormalities (hydronephrosis, neurogenic bladder). Low birth weight is also common.

Infants born to mothers with varicella in the period from 5 days prior to delivery up to 2 days after delivery are at high risk for severe neonatal varicella. They acquire the infection transplacentally.

Since the mother has not developed a strong antibody response, the infant lacks the protective effect of maternal anti-varicella-zoster virus (VZV) antibodies.  Therefore varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) should be administered as soon as possible after birth to newborns whose mothers have varicella 5 days before and up to 2 days after the delivery.

Since perinatally acquired varicella can be potentially life-threatening, the infant should typically be treated with intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) when lesions appear.

For pregnant women with uncomplicated primary varicella or herpes zoster that does not require hospitalization, the recommended treatment is oral acyclovir (800 mg five times daily for seven days).
questions.learning: 13 to 20 weeks The risk of developing fetal varicella syndrome (congenital varicella syndrome) is highest when the mother develops varicella infection between 13 to 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, and investigations reveal elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels and renal calculi. Which investigation should be performed next?
questions.explanation: The combination of abdominal pain (potentially from peptic ulcers or pancreatitis), renal calculi, and elevated Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) levels in a middle-aged female strongly suggests Primary Hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most often caused by a single parathyroid adenoma. Once the biochemical diagnosis is established, the most appropriate next step for localizing the overactive gland is a Technetium (Tc)-99m sestamibi scan. This nuclear imaging test is highly sensitive for identifying parathyroid adenomas, as they retain the tracer longer than normal thyroid tissue. USG thyroid (Option A) can visualize the thyroid but is less specific for parathyroid localization. A Dexa scan (Option C) is useful to assess bone density in hyperparathyroidism but is not a localization study. A radioactive iodine uptake test (Option D) is used to evaluate thyroid function in hyperthyroidism, not parathyroid disease. Localization is essential for surgical planning, as it allows for a minimally invasive parathyroidectomy
questions.learning: The combination of abdominal pain (potentially from peptic ulcers or pancreatitis), renal calculi, and elevated Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) levels in a middle-aged female strongly suggests Primary Hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The slogan coined by WHO 'Do it Right' in the first aid of a snake bite includes all of the following except?
options: Tell sequence of events in detail after the bite
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Incisions

Incisions are not a part of the management of a snake bite.

The first aid following a snake bite consists of the mnemonic: carry no right.

Carry: The victim is not allowed to walk, even for a short distance. Walking generates muscle-pumping activity which disperses the venom into the systemic circulation.

No: No tourniquet, no electrotherapy, no cutting, no pressure immobilization, no suction to the bite site

R: Reassure the patient since 70% of the bites are from non-venomous species.

I: Immobilize in the same way as a fractured limb. A splint can be applied to the bitten extremity to limit the movement and assist with positioning. The extremity should be maintained in a neutral position at approximately heart level.

GH: Get to a hospital immediately. The most important step is to rapidly transport the patient to a medical facility equipped to provide supportive management.

T: Tell the doctor of any systemic symptoms which may have appeared on the way to the hospital.

Note that elapid envenomations that are primarily neurotoxic and have no significant effects on local tissue may be managed by pressure immobilization. In this technique, the entire limb is immediately wrapped with a bandage and then immobilized. This technique restricts lymphatic drainage and has been shown to delay the absorption of venom into the systemic circulation. However, the offending snake should have been reliably identified as neurotoxic and the rescuer should be trained in applying this pressure bandage.
questions.learning: Incisions Incisions are not a part of the management of a snake bite. The first aid following a snake bite consists of the mnemonic: carry no right.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following can be used for developmental screening for use in community to identify children (aged 0–6 years) with developmental delay?
options: Revised Denver Development Screening Test (Denver II)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trivandrum Development Screening Chart

The Trivandrum Development Screening Chart (TDSC) is a simple, rapid developmental screening tool designed for community use to identify developmental delay in children aged 0–6 years. It is easy to administer by primary healthcare workers and is widely used in community screening programs in India.

Why not the other options?

• A. Revised Denver Development Screening Test (Denver II): Comprehensive developmental screening test but not specifically designed for community-level screening.
• B. Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3): Parent-completed screening tool; not the standard community screening tool used in India.
• C. Phatak’s Baroda Development Screening Test: Used for developmental assessment but TDSC is the preferred community screening tool for children 0–6 years.
questions.learning: Trivandrum Development Screening Chart — The Trivandrum Development Screening Chart (TDSC) is a simple, rapid developmental screening tool designed for community use to identify developmental delay in children aged 0–6 years.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Mid-year population is the denominator in?
questions.explanation: The mid-year population is commonly used as the denominator in rates that measure events occurring in the entire population over a year. The best example is the Crude Death Rate (CDR). CDR is calculated as: The mid-year population (usually estimated on 1st July) represents the average population at risk during the year, making it the most appropriate denominator. Why other options are wrong: (B) CFR (Case Fatality Rate) : Denominator = number of diagnosed cases, not total population (C) MMR (Maternal Mortality Ratio) : Denominator = live births, not population (D) NMR (Neonatal Mortality Rate) : Denominator = live births, not population
questions.learning: The mid-year population is commonly used as the denominator in rates that measure events occurring in the entire population over a year. The best example is the Crude Death Rate (CDR).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 53-year-old male patient was admitted following a road traffic accident. Paradoxical respiration was seen. His chest X-ray is shown below. He was given analgesics and oxygen was administered via face mask but he developed respiratory failure. What is the best line of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical ventilation

The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest.

It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall. Mechanical ventilation (like Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is the management of flail chest with respiratory failure.

Flail Chest :

* A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage.

* This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places.

* The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well.

Clinical Features:

On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air, therefore, moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration).

Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for the paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement, and the associated lung contusion are all causes of hypoxia and respiratory failure.

The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Treatment

* Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided

* Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) or epidural analgesia and physiotherapy.

* IPPV (Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for cases developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen.

Other options:

Option A: Chest tube drainage can be done in traumatic pulmonary contusion associated with pneumothorax or hemothorax

Option B: Intrapleural local analgesia can be given if the patient has a chest tube inserted. Since the chest tube drainage is only done after stabilising the patient, intrapleural analgesia is not the best line of treatment at this stage.

Option D: Surgical fixation of the fracture is done only in patients with severe chest injury and pulmonary contusion. Also, surgery should be proceeded only after the patient's condition is stabilised.
questions.learning: Mechanical ventilation — The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest. It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a forensic examination, the police presented a skull bone for analysis, and the cephalic index was determined to be 85. Which race does the skull likely belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mongoloids

A skull bone with a cephalic index of 85 belongs to the Mongoloid race.

Cephalic Index is used to determine the race of the individual.

Cranial index = Maximum skull breadth x 100 / Maximum skull length.

There are three main racial groups: Caucasian, Mongoloid and Negroid. All the skulls cannot be accurately differentiated into the 3 broad categories because of the racial mixing.

The skull offers the best evidence of racial origins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following hypothalamic nuclei are responsible for leptin resistance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arcuate nucleus

Leptin is the body’s “fat thermostat hormone”

• Secreted by adipocytes
• Tells the brain: “We have enough energy, stop eating.”

But in obesity- Leptin is high, yet appetite persists → leptin resistance

The arcuate nucleus is the main hypothalamic leptin-sensing center containing POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons. Leptin resistance arises from impaired signaling in this nucleus, leading to failure of appetite suppression. It integrates peripheral energy signals.

| Nucleus | Function | Lesion Effect

| ------- | -------- | -------------

| Arcuate | Leptin integration | Leptin resistance

| Lateral | Hunger center | ↓ eating

| Ventromedial | Satiety center | Hyperphagia

| Paraventricular | Autonomic/endocrine control | Dysregulation

Extra Edge Points

1. POMC → α-MSH → acts on MC4 receptor → satiety
2. NPY = strongest appetite stimulant
3. AgRP blocks melanocortin receptors → promotes eating

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the most common lacrimal gland tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pleomorphic adenoma

Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common lacrimal gland tumor. It is also the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland.

Pleomorphic adenoma, or benign mixed tumor, presents commonly in middle age as a slowly progressive painless swelling in the upper outer quadrant of the eyelid. The bone is usually not invaded in these tumors. They are treated by surgical removal along with their intact pseudo-capsule.

Malignant tumors of the lacrimal gland such as adenoid cystic carcinoma (option A), mucoepidermoid carcinoma (option C) and malignant mixed tumor (option D) generally occur in the elderly with a short history of appearance, rapid progression and pain. These tumors also present in the upper eyelid and are known to invade the adjacent bones. Radical surgical procedures and high dose radiotherapy are necessary for the removal of the tumor. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland.

Both malignant and benign tumors are known to push the eyeball downwards and inwards while restricting the upwards and outwards movement of the eyeball.

The most common epithelial tumors, in order of frequency, are as follows:

1. Benign mixed tumor (BMT), also known as a pleomorphic adenoma (PA)
2. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC)
3. Pleomorphic adenocarcinoma (ACA)
4. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
questions.learning: Pleomorphic adenoma Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common lacrimal gland tumor. It is also the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A firefighter sustains electrical burns while at work. On arrival at the ED, he is hemodynamically stable. ECG monitoring and initial fluid resuscitation are started. His urine is collected for routine lab examination and appears as below. Which of the following is most likely to be found on urine analysis?
options: Increased RBC metabolites in the urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Myoglobin

The tea-coloured urine in the clinical vignette in the setting of an electrical injury is suggestive of rhabdomyolysis following electrical burns and the substance most likely found in this urine is myoglobin.

The higher the current and voltage associated with alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC), the greater the electrical damage will be. High-voltage current (greater than 500 V to 1000 V) typically will result in deep burns, while low-voltage current (110 V to 120 V) is more likely to result in tetany. This sustained contraction can lead to muscle injury and result in rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria, presenting as tea-coloured urine.

Rhabdomyolysis is a serious complication of electrical injuries. It leads to muscle breakdown, releasing a high amount of myoglobin in the blood. Myoglobinuria can lead to acute kidney injury by the following mechanisms:

* Direct toxic effect of myoglobin and heme on the PCT.

* Tubular obstruction by precipitation of pigmented casts.

* Renal vasoconstriction can cause FeNa < 1 (unlike other renal causes of AKI).

Biochemical features of rhabdomyolysis are elevated CPK, BUN, Cr, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia.

Other causes of Rhabdomyolysis includes:

* Traumatic crush injuries

* Muscle ischemia during vascular or orthopedic surgery

* Compression during coma or immobilization

* Prolonged seizure activity

* Excessive or strenuous exercise

* Heatstroke or malignant hyperthermia

* Infections

* Metabolic disorders such as hypophosphatemia or severe hypothyroidism

* Myopathies (drug-induced, metabolic, or inflammatory).

Following resuscitation of these patient and local treatment of burns, management includes infusion of large amounts of intravenous fluids (2 mL/kg body weight per hour), alkalinization of the urine (to prevent myoglobin precipitation in renal tubules and acidosis), and mannitol (improves renal blood flow, GFR, and urine output).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant presents with a scrotal swelling that has been present since birth and is exacerbated by crying. The swelling has suddenly become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strangulated inguinal hernia

The clinical scenario of a 2-month-old male infant with a reducible scrotal swelling that is exacerbated by crying present since birth (congenital) and has become suddenly painful, red, and irreducible is most suggestive of a strangulated inguinal hernia. Infants are at high risk for incarceration of an inguinal hernia because of the narrow inguinal ring.

An inguinal hernia represents a protrusion of abdominal contents through a patent processus vaginalis into the inguinal canal and sometimes into the scrotum. It is a common indication for surgical repair in children. When a hernia becomes incarcerated and is not reducible, it can lead to strangulation of its contents.

Management of a strangulated inguinal hernia requires emergency surgical repair. It is usually performed by open inguinal repair, and a contralateral side evaluation may be considered. Laparoscopic approaches can also be used in certain cases. The repair of a patent processus vaginalis is emphasized to prevent recurrence.

Other options:

Option A: Epididymitis occurring before 6 months of age is usually due to infected urine ascending through the vas deferens. In contrast, epididymo-orchitis typically develops after puberty in sexually active boys and presents with acute testicular pain, fever, dysuria, increased frequency of urination, and urethral discharge. Pain may subside on elevation of the testis (Prehn’s sign).

Option B: Testicular torsion presents with acute scrotal pain associated with vomiting and absent cremasteric reflex.

Option D: A hydrocele refers to the accumulation of fluid between the parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis, usually limited to the scrotum. They are generally asymptomatic, non-tender, and may fluctuate in size, often decreasing overnight; they can also occur bilaterally. In infants, hydroceles may sometimes be tense and cause discomfort.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for hairy cell leukemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cladribine

Cladribine is the drug of choice in hairy cell leukemia.

Cladribine is a purine analogue with potent and curative activity against hairy cell leukemia.

Other treatment options for hairy cell leukemia include deoxycoformycin, interferon-alpha, and splenectomy. Chemotherapy-refractory patients are treated with vemurafenib, a BRAF kinase inhibitor. The addition of rituximab results in more durable remissions.

Cladribine is also used to treat CLL, low-grade lymphomas, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, cutaneous T-cell lymphomas, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

The major dose-limiting toxicity of cladribine is myelosuppression.
questions.learning: Cladribine Cladribine is the drug of choice in hairy cell leukemia. Cladribine is a purine analogue with potent and curative activity against hairy cell leukemia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radiological interventions are used in the management of cerebral aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coiling

Coiling is the radiological intervention used in the management of cerebral aneurysm.

Aneurysms occur at the bifurcations of the large to medium-sized intracranial arteries. Rupture is into the subarachnoid space in the basal cisterns. Approximately 85% of the aneurysms occur in the anterior circulation, mainly on the circle of Willis.

Most unruptured intracranial aneurysms are completely asymptomatic. When the aneurysm ruptures, 45% of cases present with sudden onset severe headache, described as the worst headache of the patient's life. Other features include neck rigidity and transient loss of consciousness.

Diagnosis -

CT shows hyperattenuating material filling the subarachnoid space. CT angiography has a high sensitivity for aneurysms and AVMs, but digital subtraction angiography remains the gold standard.

Treatment -

Early aneurysm repair prevents re-rupture. At many centers, definitive repair is carried out within 24 h of the bleed in all patients who are stable enough to tolerate the procedure. An aneurysm can be “clipped” by a neurosurgeon or “coiled” by an endovascular approach.  Surgical repair involves placing a metal clip across the aneurysm neck, thereby immediately eliminating the risk of rebleeding. This approach requires craniotomy (option D) and brain retraction, which is associated with neurologic morbidity.

Endovascular techniques involve placing platinum coils within the aneurysm via a catheter that is passed from the femoral artery. The aneurysm is packed tightly to enhance thrombosis and over time is walled off from the circulation.

Intracranial pressure should be measured and the cerebral perfusion pressure targeted at 60–70 mmHg.

Delayed cerebral ischemia remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality following aneurysmal SAH. Treatment with the calcium channel antagonist nimodipine (60 mg PO every 4 h) improves outcome, perhaps by preventing ischemic injury rather than reducing the risk of vasospasm.

The image below is an arteriogram showing a coiled aneurysm (indicated by yellow arrows) of the posterior cerebral artery with a residual aneurysmal sac.

Other options :

Option B - Sclerotherapy is used in the management of venous insufficiency.

Option D - Stenting is employed mainly for stenotic vascular lesions.
questions.learning: Coiling Coiling is the radiological intervention used in the management of cerebral aneurysm. Aneurysms occur at the bifurcations of the large to medium-sized intracranial arteries.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic alcoholism presents with skin lesions. His diet mainly consists of polished rice. Based on his clinical presentation and dietary history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A chronic alcoholic whose diet consists primarily of polished rice is at extremely high risk for Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, as the process of polishing rice removes the thiamine-rich husk. This deficiency causes Beriberi. "Dry" beriberi primarily affects the nervous system (peripheral neuropathy), while "wet" beriberi affects the heart (high-output heart failure and edema). Phrynoderma (Option A) is a "toad-skin" appearance caused by Vitamin A and essential fatty acid deficiency. Psoriasis (Option C) and Eczema (Option D) are chronic inflammatory skin conditions that are not typically caused by a nutritional deficiency of thiamine. In addition to beriberi, thiamine deficiency in alcoholics can lead to the life-threatening Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Treatment involves urgent thiamine replacement. This clinical combination of alcoholism and a polished-rice diet is a classic "textbook" description of thiamine deficiency in medical board examinations
questions.learning: A chronic alcoholic whose diet consists primarily of polished rice is at extremely high risk for Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, as the process of polishing rice removes the thiamine-rich husk.

questions.subject: Medicine

options: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue
Upsetting of receptors so no treatment is required

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient is unable to flex the hip and knee following trauma to the anterior thigh. Injury to which of the following muscles is most likely responsible for this combined deficit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sartorius

The sartorius is the only muscle that produces both hip flexion and knee flexion, as it crosses both the hip and knee joints. It originates from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and inserts into the pes anserinus on the medial surface of the proximal tibia. It is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2–L3).

Injury to the sartorius results in weakness of hip flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation, along with knee flexion, producing difficulty assuming the cross-legged (“tailor’s”) position.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rectus femoris: Flexes the hip but extends the knee; injury causes weakness of hip flexion and knee extension, not knee flexion.
• C. Tensor fasciae latae: Flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the hip and stabilizes the knee via the iliotibial tract, but does not flex the knee.
• D. Gracilis: Adducts the thigh and assists in knee flexion, but does not flex the hip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear with loss of sensation. Physical examination reveals paraesthesias with associated numbness in extremities and a raised jugular venous pressure. A thickened nerve is observed as shown in the image below. Identify the structure marked by the arrow in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater auricular nerve

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear accompanied by loss of sensation, and neck examination reveals a thickened structure suggestive of leprosy, and the thickened structure is the greater auricular nerve.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland, it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

* The anterior branch supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.

* The posterior branch supplies the skin over the mastoid process and the lower part of the back of the auricle, lobule, and concha.

Clinical considerations:

* The nerve can be thickened in conditions like leprosy and can be palpated over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image). Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerve is the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

* Cross-inervation between the somatic sensory supply (great auricular nerve) and the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland is considered an anatomical basis for the phenomenon of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct for incidence rate? 1. It is useful for taking action to control a disease. 2. Rising incidence rates may indicate ineffectiveness of the current control programmes. 3. Fluctuation in incidence rate may indicate a change in aetiology of disease. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Incidence rate measures the occurrence of new cases of a disease in a population at risk over a specified period of time. It is the best measure of the risk of developing a disease and is widely used to assess disease trends, evaluate control programs, and identify changes in disease occurrence.

• 1. It is useful for taking action to control a disease. ✓

• Incidence reflects current transmission and occurrence of new cases, making it valuable for planning and evaluating disease control measures.

• 2. Rising incidence rates may indicate ineffectiveness of the current control programmes. ✓

• An increase in incidence may suggest failure of preventive or control measures, poor vaccination coverage, or emergence of new risk factors.

• 3. Fluctuation in incidence rate may indicate a change in aetiology of disease. ✓

• Changes in incidence may result from:

• Emergence of new risk factors
• Environmental or behavioral changes
• Improved diagnostics or surveillance
• Change in the disease’s etiology

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with weakness and fatigue. Laboratory investigations reveal low hemoglobin, low reticulocyte count, and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Bone marrow examination shows a selective decrease in erythroid precursors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This question repeats the core concept from Questions 42 and 50. The clinical finding of anemia (weakness/fatigue, low Hb) with a low reticulocyte count in the presence of normal WBC and platelet counts is the hallmark of Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA). The definitive diagnostic feature is the selective reduction in erythroid precursors observed in the bone marrow analysis, while other cell lines remain healthy. Aplastic anemia (Option A) would show a decrease in all three cell lines (pancytopenia). Iron deficiency anemia (Option C) is microcytic and typically shows a low reticulocyte count but is not characterized by a total absence of erythroid precursors. Pernicious anemia (Option D), caused by B12 deficiency, is megaloblastic and also involves abnormalities in white cells and platelets. PRCA is an uncommon condition that can be associated with thymomas or autoimmune disorders

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Among the following food items, which one generally contains the highest sodium content?
questions.explanation: Among the options provided, canned soup contains the highest concentration of sodium. Processing and preservation techniques in the food industry frequently utilize significant amounts of sodium chloride and other sodium-containing preservatives (like MSG) to enhance flavor and extend shelf life. A single serving of canned soup can often exceed 50% of the recommended daily sodium intake. In contrast, natural, unprocessed foods like sugar cane (Option A), barley (Option B), and fresh fruit juices (Option D) are naturally very low in sodium. High dietary sodium is a primary risk factor for hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Clinicians often advise patients, especially those with heart or kidney conditions, to avoid processed and "canned" items in favor of fresh alternatives to manage their sodium load. Therefore, canned soup is the definitive answer for the highest sodium content among the listed foods

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and excessive hair growth. Pelvic ultrasonography reveals multiple cysts in the ovaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and hirsutism (excess hair) combined with ultrasound evidence of multiple ovarian cysts is classic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a multi-system endocrinopathy characterized by androgen excess and ovulatory dysfunction. Endometriosis (Option B) involves extra-uterine tissue growth and causes pain and infertility, but not androgenic features like acne. Hypothyroidism (Option C) can cause cycle irregularities and weight gain but is not associated with hyperandrogenism. OHSS (Option D) is an acute complication of fertility treatments presenting with sudden pain and massive ovarian enlargement rather than chronic irregular cycles. PCOS is often associated with insulin resistance and acanthosis nigricans. Diagnosis usually follows the Rotterdam criteria, requiring two out of three: oligovulation, hyperandrogenism, or polycystic ovaries on imaging
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and hirsutism (excess hair) combined with ultrasound evidence of multiple ovarian cysts is classic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following cells is responsible for the removal of small foreign particles trapped in the lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dust cells

Dust cells are responsible for the removal of small foreign particles trapped in the lungs.

Dust cells or pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAM) originate from the bone marrow and possess active phagocytic abilities. They play a role in engulfing small particles that manage to bypass the mucociliary escalator and reach the alveoli. They secrete substances that attract granulocytes to the lungs and substances that stimulate granulocyte and monocyte formation in the bone marrow. PAM function can also be detrimental—when they ingest large amounts of the substances in cigarette smoke or other irritants, they may release lysosomal products into the extracellular space to cause inflammation.

Other options:

Option A and C: Two major types of cells are found in the alveolar epithelium: Type I pneumocytes, the primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium), facilitate gas exchange and constitute the majority (95%) of the total surface area due to their flat surface. Additionally, the basement membrane of type I cells and the capillary endothelium are fused, minimizing the distance for gas diffusion and thereby facilitating gas exchange.

Type II cells, granular pneumocytes that produce surfactant, make up only 5% of the surface area in alveoli. These cells possess superoxide dismutase, making them more resistant to toxic oxygen radicals. As a result, they can survive, proliferate, and differentiate into Type I cells to restore the normal alveolar architecture

Option D: Clara cells, also known as Club cells, are specialized secretory cells found in the bronchioles that do not possess cilia. They act as progenitor cells and help in bronchial regeneration after injury. They also secrete essential defense markers and contribute to the composition of mucus through the secretion of a nonmucinous material containing carbohydrates and proteins.
questions.learning: Dust cells Dust cells are responsible for the removal of small foreign particles trapped in the lungs. Dust cells or pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAM) originate from the bone marrow and possess active phagocytic abilities.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following media is used as an enrichment medium for culturing a sputum sample from a 32-year-old man with a three-day history of fever and productive cough producing small amounts of clear sputum?
questions.explanation: The question asks for enrichment media, which are liquid media used to selectively favor the growth of a particular pathogen while inhibiting others. While the clinical scenario describes a respiratory infection, the options provided are all classic enrichment media used in microbiology. Alkaline Peptone Water (APW) (Option A) and Monsour’s TTPW (Option B) are specifically used to enrich Vibrio cholerae from stool samples. Selenite F broth (Option C) is used to enrich Salmonella and Shigella species. Although these are not standard sputum media (which would typically include Blood Agar or Chocolate Agar), they all technically fit the laboratory classification of "enrichment media." In the context of a multiple-choice question where all three listed options belong to the same functional category (enrichment media), "All of the above" is the appropriate answer regarding their classification, regardless of their specific utility for a respiratory sputum sample

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the recommended treatment for nephrotic syndrome in children?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids, such as oral prednisolone, are the first-line and mainstay treatment for nephrotic syndrome in children. This is because Minimal Change Disease (MCD) accounts for about 80% of pediatric cases and typically shows a high response rate to high-dose steroids. Remission of edema and proteinuria often occurs within 10–14 days of therapy. Steroids and cyclophosphamide (Option B) or cyclophosphamide alone (Option C) are second-line treatments reserved for children who are steroid-resistant or frequent relapsers. ACE inhibitors (Option D) are adjunctive therapies used to reduce residual proteinuria and control blood pressure but are not the primary treatment for the underlying disease. Therefore, standard initial management always begins with a steroid regimen, only escalating to immunosuppressants like cyclophosphamide if resistance develops

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy is being evaluated for possible induction or augmentation of labor using oxytocin. Considering the potential risks associated with this drug, which of the following conditions represents a contraindication to the use of oxytocin?
options: Induction of labor in post-term pregnancy
Augmentation of labor in case of slow progress
Preterm labor with cervical dilation of 3 cm
questions.explanation: The condition where the placenta covers the internal os is known as Placenta Previa (specifically Type IV/Central). This is an absolute contraindication for both vaginal delivery and the use of oxytocin. Inducing contractions in a woman with placenta previa would lead to catastrophic maternal hemorrhage as the placenta is torn during cervical changes. Induction for post-term pregnancy (Option B) and augmentation for slow progress (Option C) are the primary, standard clinical indications for oxytocin use. Preterm labor (Option D) is managed with tocolytics to stop contractions, but the presence of cervical dilation doesn't necessarily make oxytocin a direct contraindication, though it would be counterproductive unless termination is intended. Other absolute contraindications for oxytocin include a previous classical cesarean scar and active genital herpes. Proper obstetric management requires identifying the placental position via ultrasound before any attempt at induction to avoid life-threatening bleeding during the initiation of labor
questions.learning: The condition where the placenta covers the internal os is known as Placenta Previa (specifically Type IV/Central). This is an absolute contraindication for both vaginal delivery and the use of oxytocin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly patient who is a known case of scleroderma presented with shortness of breath. On examination, her right ventricular pressure was 70-80 mmHg and later on catheterization, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure was found to be 35 mmHg. Which of the following is true regarding her condition?
options: Calcium channel blockers given for all the patients
Lung transplant is the best treatment, if identified early
Lifestyle modification is the only possible approach
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endothelin receptor antagonists improves symptoms

In this elderly patient with scleroderma presenting with elevated right ventricular pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, is suggestive of scleroderma/systemic sclerosis(SSc)-associated pulmonary hypertension, and endothelin receptor antagonists improve the symptoms.

Right heart catheterization, the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension, confirms the condition when the mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) exceeds 20 mmHg. In this elderly patient with scleroderma, elevated right ventricular pressure (70-80 mmHg) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (35 mmHg) indicate severe pulmonary hypertension.

This condition involves intimal thickening and narrowing of pulmonary arteries, leading to increased blood flow resistance and symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. As the disease progresses, it causes right ventricular dysfunction, presenting as syncope, abdominal distension, ascites, and peripheral edema. The disease leads to vascular changes like intimal proliferation, fibrosis, and thrombosis, which increase right ventricular afterload and total pulmonary vascular resistance, ultimately resulting in decreased cardiac output, irreversible damage, and potential right heart failure and death.

An echocardiogram with a bubble study is an important screening test that will reveal a dilated and hypertrophied right ventricle. On chest x-ray, 'vascular pruning' may be seen as well as enlarged pulmonary arteries.

Management for pulmonary hypertension:

Note: Early identification of PAH(option B) allows for effective management with available medical therapies, making lung transplant a later option rather than the immediate treatment of choice.

Vasoreactivity testing involves the administration of inhaled nitric oxide, IV epoprostenol, IV adenosine, or inhaled iloprost. The test is considered positive if the mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAH) decreases by ≥ 10 mmHg leading to mPAH ≤ 40 mmHg, without a decrease in cardiac output (CO).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old male with T2DM presents with high grade fever and cough. He is diagnosed with COVID-19 and is admitted. He dies on the 7th day of illness. As part of surveillance, his death is recorded. What type of surveillance is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Passive

Death recorded as part of routine reporting (hospital records death, reports through standard case-reporting channels) — no active case-finding effort by health authority. Passive surveillance relies on routine, ongoing reporting by healthcare facilities/providers.

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Active | Health worker actively visits/collects data (e.g., house-to-house case search)

| Passive | Routine reporting by facilities without active seeking (this case)

| Sentinel | Selected reporting sites represent larger population trend

| Syndromic | Based on symptom clusters/patterns, before confirmed diagnosis

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60 years old male patient was undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the surgery, it was observed that there was a sudden decrease in etCO2 to 8 mm Hg, SpO2 was 90%, BP dropped to 80/50 mm Hg and peak airway pressure was observed to be 18 mm Hg. Which of the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CO2 embolism

A sudden sharp fall in EtCO₂, hypotension, mild desaturation, and normal airway pressures during laparoscopy strongly point to CO₂ embolism. Pneumothorax, bronchospasm, and endobronchial intubation all increase airway pressures, which is not seen here. CO₂ embolism is a known complication of pneumoperitoneum.
questions.learning: CO2 embolism — A sudden sharp fall in EtCO₂, hypotension, mild desaturation, and normal airway pressures during laparoscopy strongly point to CO₂ embolism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to diffuse muscle aches and weakness. He has also noticed darkening of his urine. he patient recently joined the military and was participating in rigorous training exercises in hot weather earlier in the day. Laboratory results are as follows: Sodium: 136 mEq/L Potassium: 5.6 mEq/L Bicarbonate: 18 mEq/L Creatinine: 2.0 mg/dL CK: 22,000 U/L (normal: 30-170) Which of the following urine microscopy is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Granular casts

Severe muscle injury with markedly elevated CK and dark urine after strenuous exercise indicates rhabdomyolysis. Myoglobin released from muscle causes acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and acute kidney injury.

Urine microscopy in ATN shows muddy brown granular casts formed from necrotic tubular epithelial cells and protein debris. Thus, rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI is characterized by granular casts on urine microscopy.

Why not other options:

A. Dysmorphic RBCs: Glomerulonephritis.

B. Eosinophils: Acute interstitial nephritis.

D. Waxy casts: Chronic kidney disease.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia. He developed diarrhoea two weeks ago. He was given a diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome. What is the underlying cause?
options: Demyelination of A and B fibers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Demyelination of A and B fibers

The underlying cause of Guillain-Barré syndrome is demyelination of A and B fibres.

Erlanger and Gasser classified nerve fibres into types A, B, and C, with type A fibres further subdivided into α, β, γ, and δ fibres.

* Type A fibers are the typical large- and medium-sized myelinated fibers of spinal nerves.

* Type B fibers are smaller fibres with minimal myelination. They transmit impulses of the ANS, including the bladder.

* Type C fibers are small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disease that causes fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy. It is a T-cell-mediated immune response.

GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acute gastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

It presents with the following features:

* Ascending motor paralysis (lower limbs > upper limbs)

* Sensory deficits may or may not be seen

* Deep tendon reflexes—absent

* Transient bladder dysfunction—severe cases

* Autonomic manifestations—loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias.

Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular and endoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electron microscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination induced by the actions of activated macrophages.

There are several types of Guillain–Barré syndrome:

* Demyelinating

* Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP)—most common

* Axonal

* Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)

* Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)

* Regional GBS syndromes: Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS)

Other options:

Option A and D: Spinal cord inflammation/demyelination point to conditions like transverse myelitis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which medication should be preferred for a 45-year-old chronic alcoholic with a history of liver cirrhosis, admitted with fever and abdominal pain, and found to have ascitic fluid neutrophil count of 360 cells/µL?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP), a common and serious complication of cirrhosis. SBP is diagnosed when the ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is . In this patient, the count is 360, confirming the diagnosis. Cefotaxime, a third-generation cephalosporin, is the first-line antibiotic of choice for SBP. It provides excellent coverage against common gram-negative aerobic organisms like E. coli and Klebsiella, which are the most frequent causes. Metronidazole (Option B) targets anaerobes, which are rarely involved in SBP. Amoxicillin (Option C) has poor penetration and high resistance rates in this setting. Vancomycin (Option D) is reserved for suspected MRSA or failed initial therapy. Because Cefotaxime is highly effective, has low toxicity, and is proven to improve survival in cirrhotic patients with peritonitis, it is the definitive treatment

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A healthcare worker develops a needle-stick injury from a patient suspected to have acute HIV infection. Which test can detect HIV at the earliest stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nucleic acid test (NAT)

After HIV exposure, the timeline of detectability follows the "diagnostic window" sequence:

HIV RNA (NAT) → p24 antigen → HIV antibodies

• NAT (Nucleic Acid Test) detects HIV RNA directly and becomes positive earliest — typically \~10 days post-exposure — because it detects the virus itself before the immune system has mounted any response (antigen or antibody).
• p24 antigen becomes detectable slightly later, around \~2 weeks post-exposure — it's a viral core protein that rises as viral replication ramps up, but still requires enough viral burden to be detected by the assay.
• HIV antibody tests are the last to turn positive, typically 3–4 weeks to 3 months post-exposure ("window period"), since antibody production requires time for seroconversion.
