questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Increase in glomerular capillary permeability leads to which substance appearing in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein

The glomerular filtration barrier normally prevents filtration of large, negatively charged plasma proteins, especially albumin, through its three layers:

• Fenestrated endothelium
• Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) (size- and charge-selective)
• Podocyte slit diaphragm

When this barrier becomes more permeable (e.g., glomerular disease), proteins leak into the urine, resulting in proteinuria (albuminuria).

• Protein is normally retained in the circulation. Increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier allows its passage into the urine.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glucose: Freely filtered and normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; glucosuria results from hyperglycemia or tubular dysfunction, not increased glomerular permeability.
• B. Ketone bodies: Freely filtered; ketonuria occurs in starvation or diabetic ketoacidosis.
• D. Uric acid: Freely filtered and undergoes filtration, reabsorption, and secretion; its urinary excretion is unrelated to glomerular barrier permeability.
questions.learning: Protein — The glomerular filtration barrier normally prevents filtration of large, negatively charged plasma proteins, especially albumin, through its three layers: • Fenestrated endothelium • Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) (size- and charge-selective)…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy develops recurrent hypoglycemic episodes following moderate physical activity. Investigations show increased levels of ketone bodies, lactic acid, and triglycerides, along with hepatomegaly and renomegaly on examination. Which hepatic enzyme deficiency best explains these clinical and laboratory findings?
questions.explanation: The combination of fasting-induced hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), and renomegaly (enlarged kidneys) is pathognomonic for Von Gierke’s disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) . This condition is caused by a deficiency in glucose-6-phosphatase, the enzyme responsible for converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose during glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Without this enzyme, the liver cannot release glucose into the blood, leading to severe hypoglycemia and the shunting of metabolites into pathways that produce lactic acid, triglycerides, and ketone bodies. Option B and C are metabolic intermediates, not enzymes whose deficiency causes this syndrome. Option D refers to complex carbohydrates involved in different storage disorders (mucopolysaccharidoses). Therefore, the inability to perform the final step of glucose release due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is the definitive enzymatic cause of this patient’s multi-system metabolic derangement
questions.learning: The combination of fasting-induced hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), and renomegaly (enlarged kidneys) is pathognomonic for Von Gierke’s disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) .

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old female came to the hospital with a history of trauma to the ear. On examination, there is swelling, tenderness, and discoloration of the ear. Which of the following is false regarding the given image?
options: All cases should receive prophylactic antibiotic
Caused by accumulation of blood in perichondrial space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resolves spontaneously

The given clinical history of trauma to the ear along with swelling, tenderness, and discoloration of the pinna is highly suggestive of hematoma of the auricle (perichondrial hematoma). It does not resolve spontaneously.

It is a collection of blood between the auricular cartilage and its perichondrium known as perichondrial space (Option C). It is commonly seen in boxers, wrestlers, and rugby players due to blunt trauma and can result in a deformity called cauliflower ear, wrestler's ear, or pugilistic ear (Option B). Severe perichondritis may occur if the hematoma gets infected.

All cases should receive prophylactic antibiotics (Option A). Aspiration of the hematoma under strict aseptic precautions and a pressure dressing is done to prevent reaccumulation. Aspiration may need to be repeated. When aspiration fails, incision and drainage should be done.
questions.learning: Resolves spontaneously — The given clinical history of trauma to the ear along with swelling, tenderness, and discoloration of the pinna is highly suggestive of hematoma of the auricle (perichondrial hematoma).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A cattle farmer presented with a lesion on the arm. Gram staining showed gram-positive rods with square ends with a central spore. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacillus anthracis

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis.

Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive rod with square ends giving it a characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance.

Bacillus anthracis is a large, gram-positive, endospore-forming (non-bulging spores), rod-shaped bacterium. It causes zoonotic infections in humans. It is non-motile and capsulated with a characteristic polypeptide capsule.

The image shows the characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance of bacillus anthracis on Gram staining.

Bacillus anthracis is a category A bioterrorism agent which can cause:

* Cutaneous anthrax: It is caused by contact with infected animal/ animal products. It is seen in tanners and hide-porters. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The lesion is also called a malignant pustule. The majority of the patients recover spontaneously, but a few may succumb to septicemia or meningitis.

* Pulmonary anthrax: It is caused by inhaling spores. It is seen in wool sorters. The infection from the lung spreads to the mediastinal lymph nodes and causes hemorrhagic mediastinitis and sepsis.

* Intestinal anthrax: It is caused rarely, by ingesting infected animals.

The image below shows necrotic eschar seen in anthrax:

Laboratory diagnosis:

* Microscopy of the smears shows bacilli arranged end to end in the form of long chains. This is called bamboo stick appearance.

* Under the low-power microscope, the edge of the colony is composed of long, interlacing chains of bacilli, resembling locks of matted hair, called Medusa head appearance.

Fluid or pus from cutaneous lesions, pleural fluid, blood, or CSF can be cultured on:

* Nutrient agar- frosted glass appearance

* Gelatin stab culture- Inverted fir tree appearance

* Blood agar- Non-hemolytic colonies

* Solid medium with penicillin- String of pearls appearance

Other options:

Option A: Infection with Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning with a longer incubation period of 8-16 hours. But patients usually have a history of consumption of fried rice.

Option C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenting bacteria that shows swarming motility. Diseases caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa:

* Burns infections

* Opportunistic and nosocomial infections

* Shanghai fever: severe enteric disease and sepsis

* Malignant otitis externa in diabetics

* Jacuzzi syndrome (Hot tub folliculitis)

* Ecthyma gangrenosum

* Green-nail syndrome

Option D: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products from goats, sheep, cattle, pigs, and other animals. Clinically, patients may present with an acute infection comprised of undulant fever (Rising and falling fever). They may also have arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.
questions.learning: Bacillus anthracis — The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive rod with square ends giving it a characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with dysphagia, retrosternal pain, and postprandial regurgitation often accompanied by coughing. Based on these symptoms, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of dysphagia, retrosternal pain, and specifically regurgitation accompanied by coughing after meals is highly characteristic of Esophageal diverticula (Option C), such as Zenker’s diverticulum. The regurgitation of undigested food trapped in the diverticulum pouch often leads to aspiration and coughing. Achalasia (Option B) presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss, with regurgitation occurring more distantly from meals. Reflux esophagitis (Option D) causes heartburn (pyrosis) but less frequently causes mechanical regurgitation leading to immediate post-prandial coughing. Brown-Patterson-Kelly (Option A), or Plummer-Vinson syndrome, presents with a triad of dysphagia, iron-deficiency anemia, and esophageal webs. Therefore, the specific mechanical symptoms described point definitively to the presence of a diverticular pouch. Diagnosis is confirmed by a barium swallow showing the anatomical outpouching. Consequently, esophageal diverticula is the most probable diagnosis for this combination of symptoms
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of dysphagia, retrosternal pain, and specifically regurgitation accompanied by coughing after meals is highly characteristic of Esophageal diverticula (Option C), such as Zenker’s diverticulum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient complains of experiencing pain in the calf region after walking a certain distance. He reports that he needs to rest to relieve the pain. Which grade of Boyd's grading system does this symptom correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Grade 3

This patient's pain typically resolves with rest. This indicates that he can be classified as Grade III according to Boyd's classification of claudication.

Boyd's grading system is commonly used to classify the severity of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) based on the presence and severity of symptoms.

Grade III corresponds to symptoms of intermittent claudication, where the patient experiences reproducible muscle pain, cramping, or weakness in the lower limbs (usually the calf muscles) after a specific distance of walking or physical activity. The pain typically resolves with rest. Grade III indicates moderate PAD severity.

Boyd's classification of claudication:

* Grade I: Patient complains of pain after walking. If the patient continues to walk, due to increased blood flow in muscle and opening of collaterals metabolites causing pain are washed away and the pain subsides.

* Grade II: Pain still persists on continuing to walk; but can walk with effort.

* Grade III: The patient has to rest to relieve the pain.

* Grade IV: Pain at rest.
questions.learning: Grade 3 — This patient's pain typically resolves with rest. This indicates that he can be classified as Grade III according to Boyd's classification of claudication.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the predictive factors for Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR)? I. Low level of maternal 1st trimester Beta hCG II. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks of pregnancy III. Fetal echogenic bowel on ultrasound IV. Maternal medical disorder Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

The following are important predictors of FGR:

• II. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks of pregnancy: Increased uterine artery resistance, persistent notching, or elevated pulsatility index indicates impaired placentation and is a strong predictor of early-onset FGR and preeclampsia.
• III. Fetal echogenic bowel on ultrasound: Echogenic bowel is associated with FGR, congenital infections (especially CMV), chromosomal abnormalities, cystic fibrosis, and fetal bowel pathology.
• IV. Maternal medical disorder: Maternal conditions such as:

• Chronic hypertension
• Preeclampsia
• Diabetes with vascular disease
• Chronic kidney disease
• Autoimmune disorders (e.g., SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome) significantly increase the risk of FGR.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. Low level of maternal first-trimester β-Hcg: Low β-hCG is not an established predictor of FGR. More useful first-trimester biochemical markers include low Pregnancy-Associated Plasma Protein-A (PAPP-A) and low Placental Growth Factor (PlGF).
questions.learning: II, III and IV — The following are important predictors of FGR: • II. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks of pregnancy: Increased uterine artery resistance, persistent notching, or elevated pulsatility index indicates impaired placentation and…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In the image shown, identify the function of the marked structure on the endotracheal tube.
options: Prevention of air leakage and aspiration
Suctioning of lower respiratory tract secretions
questions.explanation: The marked structure on the endotracheal tube (ET) is the inflatable cuff. Its primary function is to create a physical seal between the tube and the tracheal wall once it is inflated with air. This seal serves two critical purposes: it ensures that positive pressure ventilation is efficient by preventing air leakage around the tube, and it protects the airway from aspiration by blocking secretions or vomit from entering the lower respiratory tract. Monitoring airway pressure (Option B) is done through the ventilator circuit, and suctioning secretions (Option D) requires a separate suction catheter. Visualization of the vocal cords (Option A) is achieved using a laryngoscope during the initial intubation. Proper cuff pressure management (typically 20–30 cm H₂O) is essential to prevent tracheal mucosal ischemia
questions.learning: The marked structure on the endotracheal tube (ET) is the inflatable cuff. Its primary function is to create a physical seal between the tube and the tracheal wall once it is inflated with air.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male has been diagnosed with achalasia cardia through esophageal manometry. The manometry results reveal simultaneous, high-pressure contractions in the distal esophagus, along with spasmodic contractions. What type of achalasia does this patient's presentation correspond among the provided options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type III

The classification of achalasia into types I, II, and III is based on the Chicago Classification. This system uses high-resolution manometry to categorize esophageal motility disorders.

| Type of Achalasia | Description | Notes

| ----------------- | ----------- | -----

| Type I (Classic Achalasia) | Minimal to no esophageal body peristalsis and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing. | Also known as "minimal contractility" achalasia.

| Type II (Compression Achalasia) | Intermittent periods of pan-esophageal pressurization (> 20% of swallows) due to some preserved but uncoordinated esophageal body peristalsis and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. | Good response to therapy.

| Type III (Spastic Achalasia) | Spastic contractions in the distal esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. | Least common type. Often harder to treat and may require more aggressive therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following drugs causes carcinoma bladder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyclophosphamide

Cyclophosphamide (an alkylating agent) causes bladder cancer

The risk of bladder cancer with cyclophosphamide is directly proportional to the duration and intensity of cyclophosphamide treatment. Phosphoramide mustard is the primary mutagenic metabolite that causes bladder cancer in patients exposed to cyclophosphamide.

Painless, gross hematuria is the most common symptom that is indicative of a bladder carcinoma until proven otherwise.

Depending upon the depth of invasion, bladder carcinoma can be divided into

1. Flat, non-invasive carcinoma in situ (CIS)
2. Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (70% of cases) - does not invade detrusor muscle but can invade lamina propria.
3. Muscle-invasive bladder cancer - invades the detrusor muscle.

Diagnosis is by cystourethroscopy (directly visualizing the growth) and biopsy. Management is as follows:

1. Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer:

1. Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed by intravesical chemotherapy with mitomycin C or epirubicin
2. Immunotherapy with regular intravesical instillations of Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) in high-risk tumors.

2. Muscle invasive bladder cancer: Radical cystectomy along with urinary diversion procedure and lymph node dissection +/- neoadjuvant chemotherapy

Other options:

Option B: Cisplatin is an anticancer drug used to treat testicular cancer. It is associated with an increased risk for acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Option C: Taxane is an anticancer drug and is the main component in the treatment regimens of metastatic cancers. Taxane's adverse effects are neutropenia and fluid retention (pulmonary edema).

Option D: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) and is used in the treatment of estrogen-dependent breast cancer. Due to its partial agonistic activity, it is known to increase endometrial cancer in post-menopausal women.
questions.learning: Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide (an alkylating agent) causes bladder cancer The risk of bladder cancer with cyclophosphamide is directly proportional to the duration and intensity of cyclophosphamide treatment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The serum level of tetanus antitoxin that gives clinical protection is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. >0.01 IU/ml

The serum level of tetanus antitoxin that gives clinical protection is 0.01 IU/ml.

Tetanus is best prevented by tetanus toxoid. It provides active immunization by stimulating the production of protective antitoxin. Vaccination should be aimed at maintaining the serum protective level of antitoxin (approximately 0.01 IU/ml) throughout life and covering the entire community.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions leads to a leftward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve describes the relationship between oxygen partial pressure and hemoglobin saturation. A leftward shift indicates an increased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, meaning oxygen is bound more tightly and released less easily to tissues. Alkalosis (Option C), which is an increase in blood pH, is a classic cause of this leftward shift. Hypoxia (Option A) does not directly shift the curve but triggers physiological responses. Hypercarbia (increased ) (Option B), an increase in temperature, and an increase in 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) (Option D) all cause a rightward shift in the curve, decreasing oxygen affinity to facilitate delivery to tissues during high metabolic demand. This rightward movement is known as the Bohr effect. Because alkalosis increases the attraction between hemoglobin and oxygen, it is the only factor listed that definitively causes a leftward shift in the curve

questions.text: Identify the procedure done in the labor room?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cardiotocography

The given procedure is cardiotocography (CTG; electronic fetal monitor).

CTG, is a type of intrapartum fetal monitoring where the fetal heartbeat and the uterine contractions are recorded simultaneously.

The CTG graph can be differentiated from non stress test (NST) graph by the presence of two graphical representations in CTG:

• FHR represented by the upper graph
• Uterine contractions represented by the lower graph.

NST has a single graphical representation.

A normal CTG graph is defined by the following parameters:

• Baseline FHR-110-160
• Beat to beat variability of 5-25 bpm
• Two or more Acceleration during 20 minute period
• No late deceleration
• No variable deceleration
• Early deceleration +/-

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes are involved in gluconeogenesis? A. Pyruvate carboxylase B. Phosphoenol pyruvate kinase C. Hexokinase D. Pyruvate kinase E. Glucose 6 phosphatase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A and E only

Among the given options, A and E are correct. Pyruvate carboxylase and Glucose-6-phosphatase are enzymes used in gluconeogenesis.

Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are 2 metabolic pathways in opposite directions (glucose being the substrate and product respectively). But a few reactions are not reversible in glycolysis. So a different pathway is used or a different enzyme is used by the body to make the reactions feasible.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is shown in the image below (circled)?
questions.explanation: The circled area in the CT scan represents the Osteomeatal Complex (OMC), a critical anatomical region in the lateral nasal wall. It is the common drainage pathway where the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses empty into the middle meatus. Obstruction of the OMC is a primary cause of chronic rhinosinusitis and is the focus of Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS). The columella (Option A) is the external fleshy tissue separating the nostrils. The nasal valve (Option C) is the narrowest internal part of the nasal airway that regulates airflow. The crest of the maxilla (Option D) is a bony ridge on the floor of the nasal cavity. Precise identification of the OMC on imaging is essential for preoperative surgical planning

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives for the past 6 months presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea. What would be the best method of assessing the gestational age of this patient?

LMP- Last menstrual period

USG- Ultrasonography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crown rump length by USG

The best method of assessing the gestational age of a patient on oral contraceptives with 6 weeks of amenorrhea is by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) using ultrasonography.

Gestational age refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the LMP. It is usually expressed in weeks. Following the use of oral contraceptives, ovulation may have been later than 2 weeks after the LMP. Therefore, gestational age calculated with the help of LMP will be inaccurate.

First-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL is the best method to assess gestational age. It is measured from the vertex to the coccyx.

• CRL (in mm) + 6.5 = gestational age in weeks (or)
• CRL (in mm) + 42 days = gestational age in days.

CRL measurement is shown in the image below:

Ultrasonographic parameters for estimation of the gestational age according to the trimester are as follows:

Trimester

Parameter

1st

Crown-rump length (CRL)

2nd and 3rd

• Biparietal diameter (BPD)
• Abdominal Circumference (AC)
• Head Circumference (HC)
• Femur Length. (FL)

Other options:

Option B: Adding 280 days to the LMP will provide the expected delivery date (EDD). Adding 9 months + 7 days to the LMP or 280 days to the LMP is Naegele’s formula for calculating the EDD.

Option C: Measurement of fundal height in cm (with a variation of 1-2cm) is roughly equal to the gestational age in weeks, after 24 weeks of pregnancy. This is measured from the superior border of the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterine fundus when the bladder is empty.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient develops bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea after receiving intravenous irritant substances. These clinical features are mediated by a specific reflex mechanism. Which reflex is primarily responsible for these physiological responses?
questions.explanation: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is characterized by the clinical triad of bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea (or shallow breathing). It is triggered by the stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors (C-fibers) located in the ventricular walls of the heart. Chemical irritants, certain drugs, or myocardial ischemia can activate these receptors, leading to an increase in parasympathetic (vagal) outflow and a decrease in sympathetic tone. The Bainbridge reflex (Option B) is the opposite; it causes an increase in heart rate in response to increased venous return and atrial stretch. The Cushing reflex (Option C) is a physiological response to increased intracranial pressure, characterized by hypertension, irregular breathing, and bradycardia. While both Cushing and Bezold-Jarisch involve bradycardia, the specific combination of hypotension and apnea following IV irritant administration is diagnostic for the Bezold-Jarisch reflex. This reflex can be particularly significant during anesthesia or in the early stages of a myocardial infarction
questions.learning: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is characterized by the clinical triad of bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea (or shallow breathing). It is triggered by the stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors (C-fibers) located in the ventricular walls of the heart.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common route of the spread of retinoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Direct invasion

Direct invasion is the most common mode of spread of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma arises from the neurosensory retina. It is a proliferation of neural cells that have failed to evolve normally. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.  Tumours are composed of small basophilic cells (retinoblasts), with large hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm.

It is of 4 types:

1. Endophytic (into the vitreous)with seeding of tumor cells throughout the eye
2. Exophytic (into the subretinal space) leading to retinal detachment
3. Mixed type
4. Retinocytoma: retina may be diffusely infiltrated
questions.learning: Direct invasion Direct invasion is the most common mode of spread of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma arises from the neurosensory retina.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a town with one lakh population (1,00,000) there are a total of 2500 live births in a year. There were 75 total deaths of children before the age of one month, total 200 deaths before the age of one year, and a total 300 deaths before the age of three years. Which of the following statements regarding Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) of the town for the given year are correct? 1. The denominator is 1,00,000. 2. The IMR of the town is higher than the current national average of IMR for India. 3. The numerator is the number of children dying before the age of one month. 4. The IMR of the town is 80 per 1000 live births. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 4 only

Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is defined as: Number of deaths of infants (<1 year of age) during a year ÷ Number of live births during the same year × 1000

Calculation:

• Infant deaths (<1 year) = 200
• Live births = 2500

IMR = (200 ÷ 2500) × 1000 = 80 per 1000 live births

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. The denominator is 1\,00\,000❌: Incorrect. The denominator is 2500 live births, not the total population.
• 2. The IMR of the town is higher than the current national average of IMR for India✔️: Correct. 80/1000 is much higher than the current national average.
• 3. The numerator is the number of children dying before the age of one month❌: Incorrect. The numerator is deaths before 1 year of age (200).
• 4. The IMR of the town is 80 per 1000 live births:✔️: Correct.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with complete inability to move the eyes in any direction, indicating paralysis of all extraocular muscles. Where is the lesion most likely located to cause this global ophthalmoplegia?
questions.explanation: Extraocular muscle movements are controlled by three cranial nerves: the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), and abducens (CN VI). The nuclei for these nerves are located within the brainstem. Specifically, the CN III and CN IV nuclei are in the midbrain, while the CN VI nucleus is in the pons. A significant lesion involving both the midbrain and the pons would disrupt the origins of all these motor nerves, resulting in total ophthalmoplegia (the inability to move the eyes in any direction). The frontal eye field (Option A) is responsible for initiating voluntary conjugate horizontal gaze; a lesion there causes gaze deviation, not total paralysis. The cerebral surface (Option B) handles higher visual processing, and the spinal cord (Option D) has no role in eye movement. Therefore, because the entire lower motor neuron control system for the eyes resides in the brainstem, a midbrain-pons lesion is the definitive anatomical site
questions.learning: Extraocular muscle movements are controlled by three cranial nerves: the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), and abducens (CN VI). The nuclei for these nerves are located within the brainstem.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In a patient with prostate cancer, a bone scan shows a superscan pattern characterized by diffusely increased skeletal uptake with reduced or absent splenic activity. What is the underlying reason for this superscan appearance?
options: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney
questions.explanation: In nuclear medicine, a "Super Scan" on a bone scintigraphy (using Technetium-99m MDP) occurs when there is extremely high, uniform skeletal uptake of the radiotracer. This results in a very high bone-to-soft-tissue ratio, which characteristically makes the kidneys and bladder faint or invisible (Option D is a result, not the primary "reason"). In a patient with prostate cancer, the primary reason for this appearance is diffuse osteoblastic metastasis (Option A). The metastatic cancer cells overstimulate bone turnover across nearly the entire skeleton, "grabbing" the tracer before it can be excreted by the kidneys. Option B is technically incorrect because the tracer is taken up by the reactive bone around the cancer, not the cancer cells themselves. Option C is a general description lacking the underlying pathological context. Therefore, the "super scan" in prostate cancer is a hallmark of widespread, advanced skeletal metastatic involvement
questions.learning: In nuclear medicine, a "Super Scan" on a bone scintigraphy (using Technetium-99m MDP) occurs when there is extremely high, uniform skeletal uptake of the radiotracer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP), sentinel surveillance is conducted for which diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HIV, Hepatitis B

Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP), sentinel surveillance is conducted for HIV and Hepatitis B.

The main purpose of the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) is to detect early warning signals of outbreaks.

IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Project) is a national decentralised state-based surveillance program. The mission is to detect early warning signals for timely and effective public health action so that it can be initiated against outbreaks of prone diseases in both urban and rural areas. It also provides essential data to monitor ongoing disease control programs.

The program includes a Central Surveillance Unit, State Surveillance Units, and District Surveillance Units. It collects weekly disease surveillance data on epidemic-prone diseases from reporting units such as hospitals and medical colleges. The data is analysed for disease trends and investigated by a Rapid Response Team consisting of specialists whenever there is a rising trend of illness.

The surveillance is necessary to recognize cases or clusters of cases, access the public health impact of health events, demonstrate the need for public health intervention programs, monitor the effectiveness of prevention and control measures, and identify high-risk groups or geographical areas for targeted interventions.

A total of 13 diseases both communicable and non-communicable have been included for the surveillance as per the decision of the IDSP committee. These have been grouped as per the types of surveillance into:

* Regular surveillance

* Sentinel surveillance

* Regular periodic surveys

From which Sentinel surveillance includes diseases like:

* HIV

* HBV

* HCV

and other conditions like Water Quality and Outdoor Air Quality(Large Urban Centres)
questions.learning: HIV, Hepatitis B Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP), sentinel surveillance is conducted for HIV and Hepatitis B. The main purpose of the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) is to detect early warning signals of outbreaks.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with a lump in her left breast. Examination reveals a 6 X 4 cm mass in her left breast and a single mobile lymph node palpable under the mass. Which of the following is the best-recommended surgical treatment modality in this case?
options: Modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of carcinoma of the breast. This patient has breast cancer at T3N1M0 disease which belongs to stage III A. The preferred treatment of choice in such patients is modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Pre-operative chemotherapy and postoperative radiotherapy will add to the benefit of the patients. Considerations for treatment of Stage III A and III B disease are summarized in the flowchart as shown below.

The treatment of breast cancer should be individualized and based on various clinical factors. However, a general idea of it is as follows.

When systemic adjuvant therapy is given before the surgery it is called neoadjuvant therapy.

Early-stage localised cancer(stages 0, I , II) can be treated by mastectomy or breast-conserving therapy(BCT). BCT requires radiation to further improve patient benefit.

Locally advanced breast cancer(stages IIIA, IIIB) breast adenocarcinoma without distant metastases. It includes breast cancer that fulfils any of the following criteria in the absence of distant metastasis (M0):

*

Tumours more than 5 cm in size with regional lymphadenopathy: T3, N1-3

*

Tumours of any size with direct extension to the chest wall or skin, or both (including ulcer, oedema or satellite nodules): Any T4

*

Presence of clinically fixed or matted axillary lymph nodes, or any infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or internal mammary lymphadenopathy: Any N2 or Any N3

LABC is treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy + modified radical mastectomy + adjuvant radiation therapy. If ER/PR receptor positivity is present then hormonal therapy is added, and if Her-2/neu receptor positivity is present, then Trastuzumab / Herceptin is added.

Metastatic cancer(stage IV) Treatment of metastatic cancer is aimed at palliating symptoms, improving quality of life, preventing potential disabling complications and attempting to prolong life.

Pearl PF1896: Important surgeries for breast cancer

* Tylectomy: Excision of lump

* Simple mastectomy: Palpable extent of breast + Nipple–areola complex + overlying skin.

* Subcutaneous mastectomy: Palpable extent of breast without overlying skin.

* Total mastectomy: All breast tissue + Nipple–areola complex + skin.

* Extended simple mastectomy: Simple mastectomy + removal of level I axillary lymph nodes.

* Modified radical mastectomy:  Entire breast tissue + Nipple–areola complex + skin + Axillary lymph nodes (Levels I + II ± III)

* Patey’s: Pectoralis minor is removed

* Scanlon’s: Pectoralis minor incised

* Auchincloss: Pectoralis minor only retracted

* Halsted’s radical mastectomy: Entire breast tissue + Nipple–areola complex + skin + Levels I + II+ III Axillary lymph nodes + Pectoralis major and minor

* Extended radical (Urban) - Halsted’s + Internal mammary lymph nodes

* Extended radical (Dahl-Iversion) mastectomy – Halsted’s + Internal mammary + Supraclavicular lymph nodes

* Super radical mastectomy – Halsted’s + Internal mammary + Supraclavicular + Mediastinal lymph nodes

Pearl PF2291: Contraindications for Breast Conservative Surgery

Absolute contraindications:

* 1st-trimester pregnancy

* Diffuse microcalcifications

* Persistently positive pathologic margin

* Multicentric tumor

Relative contraindications:

* Connective tissue disorders like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE),  scleroderma and rheumatoid arthritis

* Large lump-to-breast ratio, i.e., a big lump in small breast

* Lump beneath the nipple-areola complex

* Multifocal tumor

* History of therapeutic radiation exposure to the chest wall

NOTE : Some authorities do not consider Rheumatoid Arthritis as a relative contraindication as the data on radiation toxicity in RA is sparse.
questions.learning: Modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy The given clinical vignette is suggestive of carcinoma of the breast. This patient has breast cancer at T3N1M0 disease which belongs to stage III A.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with a history of complex endometrial hyperplasia, an endometrial thickness of 14 mm, an adnexal mass, and atypical cells on evaluation?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypical cells and an endometrial thickness of 14mm significantly increases the risk of underlying endometrial carcinoma. The presence of a concurrent adnexal mass in this clinical context strongly suggests the spread of the malignancy to the ovary. Metastasis from endometrial cancer is a well-recognized cause of secondary ovarian tumors. Struma ovarii (Option A) is a rare specialized germ cell tumor containing thyroid tissue, which does not correlate with endometrial hyperplasia. Polycystic ovarian disease (Option C) presents with chronic anovulation and polycystic morphology on USG, not typically an adnexal mass alongside complex atypical hyperplasia. Immature ovarian teratoma (Option D) is a germ cell malignancy seen in younger patients and lacks the direct association with thickened endometrium. Thus, given the uterine pathology, metastatic endometrial cancer to the ovary is the most probable clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient's history of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypical cells and an endometrial thickness of 14mm significantly increases the risk of underlying endometrial carcinoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has lost sensation over the dorsum of the foot and medial 4 toes. There is associated difficulty of eversion of the foot. Which nerve injury is likely to be the reason for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superficial peroneal nerve

Loss of sensation/paresthesia/numbness in the dorsum of the foot along with loss of eversion of the foot is due to injury to the superficial peroneal nerve.

The peroneus longus (principle evertor of the foot) in the lateral compartmentof the leg, is innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve. Damage to the superficial peroneal nerve would result in loss of eversion at the sub-talar joint.

The lateral compartment of the leg is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. It consists of peroneus longus and peroneus brevis.

Other options:

* Foot drop occurs due to common peroneal nerve injury and sensory loss would involve the front and outer half of the leg and the whole dorsum of the foot. A high stepping gait is seen in this nerve injury.

* The posterior tibial nerve will involve loss of sensation over the sole of the foot. This is also the nerve involved in tarsal tunnel syndrome.

* The deep peroneal nerve innervates all muscles of the anterior compartment which are the dorsiflexors of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei muscles, and skin between great and second toes.
questions.learning: Superficial peroneal nerve Loss of sensation/paresthesia/numbness in the dorsum of the foot along with loss of eversion of the foot is due to injury to the superficial peroneal nerve.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a police investigation, skeletal remains are recovered from a crime scene. Which forensic test would be most useful in distinguishing human bones from those of a dog?
questions.explanation: When skeletal remains are found, the first task of the forensic anthropologist is to determine if the bones are human or animal. The Precipitin test is a standard serological test used to identify the species of origin for biological materials, including bone extracts. It works by reacting the unknown sample with species-specific anti-sera; a positive reaction (precipitation) confirms the presence of proteins from that specific species (e.g., human). Acid-phosphatase (Option B) is used to screen for semen. LDH (Option C) is an enzyme marker of tissue damage. The Teichmann test (Option D) is used to confirm the presence of blood by forming hemin crystals. Differentiating human from canine (dog) bones is a routine requirement in forensic investigations to determine if a full criminal inquiry is warranted. While gross anatomical features often distinguish the two, the Precipitin test provides definitive biochemical proof of the species
questions.learning: When skeletal remains are found, the first task of the forensic anthropologist is to determine if the bones are human or animal. The Precipitin test is a standard serological test used to identify the species of origin for biological materials, including…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Attributable risk calculated to understand the relation between smoking and lung cancer is 90%. Which of the following is true?
options: 10% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated
90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in population if smoking is eliminated
90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated
10% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in population if smoking is eliminated
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated

Attributable risk (AR) describes the extent of outcome (lung cancer) that can be attributed to exposure (smoking). In the given scenario, an AR of 90% means that 90% of lung cancer cases among smokers are attributable to smoking. Therefore, 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated.

AR is the difference in incidence rates of disease between an exposed group and an unexposed group. AR is indicative of the extent of the disease attributed to the exposure. It also refers to the amount of disease that could be eliminated in the exposed persons if the exposure is controlled or eliminated. It also helps to determine the impact a successful preventive or public health program might have in case the exposure to cause is reduced or eliminated.

Population-attributable risk (PAR) is the difference in the incidence of disease in the total population and the incidence of disease among those not exposed to the supposed cause. PAR is useful in providing an estimate of the amount by which the disease could be reduced in that whole population if the suspected factor was eliminated or modified.

For example, a PAR of 90% in the context of smoking and lung cancer means that 90% cases of lung cancer in the population can be attributed to smoking.

Relative risk is defined as the ratio of incidence of the disease (outcome) among exposed and unexposed groups. It helps in establishing the association between a cause and a disease. However, it does not help in assessing the extent of the cause bringing about the disease (outcome).
questions.learning: 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated Attributable risk (AR) describes the extent of outcome (lung cancer) that can be attributed to exposure (smoking).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of these is not a test for the measurement of ovarian reserve?
options: Serum FSH in the early follicular phase
Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase

Ovarian reserve tests reflect quantity of remaining follicles. Day-2/3 FSH, AMH, and Antral Follicle Count are validated markers. Ovarian reserve refers to the quantity and functional capacity of the remaining ovarian follicles and predicts response to ovarian stimulation in infertility treatment. Estradiol (E2), though measured in the early follicular phase, is not a reliable ovarian-reserve indicator—levels fluctuate and can even appear normal despite diminished reserve by suppressing FSH. Hence option D is not a true ovarian reserve test.

1. Serum FSH (Day 2–3 of Cycle)

Measured in the early follicular phase (Day 2–3).

Principle

If ovarian reserve decreases → ovaries respond poorly → FSH increases due to reduced negative feedback.

| FSH Level | Interpretation

| --------- | --------------

| <10 IU/L | Normal ovarian reserve

| 10–15 IU/L | Reduced reserve

| >15 IU/L | Poor reserve

2. Antral Follicle Count (AFC)

Number of 2–10 mm follicles seen in ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound.

| AFC | Interpretation

| --- | --------------

| >15 | Good reserve

| 8–15 | Normal

| <5 | Poor ovarian reserve

3. Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)

Produced by:

Granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles.

Advantages

• Most reliable ovarian reserve marker
• Cycle independent
• Declines with age

| AMH Level | Interpretation

| --------- | --------------

| >3.5 ng/mL | High reserve / PCOS

| 1–3.5 ng/mL | Normal

| <1 ng/mL | Low ovarian reserve
questions.learning: Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase Ovarian reserve tests reflect quantity of remaining follicles. Day-2/3 FSH, AMH, and Antral Follicle Count are validated markers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A post-menopausal woman presented with pain in her lower abdomen for the past 4 months. She was informed to have fibroids for a long time. The radiological investigation is shown below. What is the type of degeneration that occurred in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Calcific degeneration

The X-ray shows calcified fibroids and is due to the calcific degeneration of fibroids.

Calcific or calcareous degeneration most often involves subserous fibroid with small pedicle or myomas in post menopausal women.

In calcareous degeneration, phosphates and carbonates of lime are deposited in the periphery along the course of the vessels. The best examples of calcareous myomas are those in old patients with long-standing myomas. They are like ‘womb-stones’ in graveyards.

Another radiograph showing large calcified myoma:

*

*

*

*

*

*

*

*

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The "dilapidated brick wall" appearance is classically seen in the histopathology of the following?
questions.explanation: The "dilapidated brick wall" appearance is a pathognomonic histopathological term used to describe Hailey-Hailey disease (Benign Familial Pemphigus) (Option A) . This genetic disorder is characterized by widespread acantholysis (loss of cell-to-cell adhesion) throughout the entire epidermis. On microscopy, the partially detached keratinocytes resemble a crumbling or dilapidated wall. Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B) also features acantholysis but it is typically suprabasal, resulting in a "tombstone" appearance of the basal layer. Darier’s disease (Option C) is characterized by dyskeratosis with "corps ronds" and "grains." Bullous pemphigoid (Option D) involves a subepidermal split without acantholysis. Because the "dilapidated wall" specifically describes the extensive, irregular epidermal detachment seen in this familial condition, Hailey-Hailey is the definitive diagnosis. It typically presents with recurrent blisters and erosions in the skin folds (axilla/groin). Understanding these distinct histological patterns is crucial for differentiating various immunobullous and genetic skin disorders
questions.learning: The "dilapidated brick wall" appearance is a pathognomonic histopathological term used to describe Hailey-Hailey disease (Benign Familial Pemphigus) (Option A) .

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the maneuver being performed in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Head tilt, chin lift

The maneuver being performed in the given image is that of head-tilt chin-lift. It is an important technique in emergency airway management to open up the airway.

Basic life support involves early recognition and management of emergencies such as heart attack, stroke, and foreign body airway obstruction. The sequence of BLS is circulation (chest compression), airway, and then breathing.

The airway is usually obstructed by posterior displacement of the tongue or epiglottis. One hand (palm) is placed on the patient’s forehead applying pressure to tilt the head back. Simultaneously, the chin is lifted with the forefinger and index finger of the opposite hand. This causes cervical flexion with an atlantooccipital extension (sniffing position). This lifts the tongue from the back of the throat.

Head-tilt chin-lift should not be performed in a patient with suspected cervical injury.

Other options:

Option B: Jaw thrust- Both hands of the clinician are placed on either side of the patient’s head and the angles of the jaw are grasped and lifted. It can be performed in a patient with cervical injury but caution must be followed to not hyperextend the neck.

Option D: Manual inline stabilization is a maneuver that limits external head and neck movement in patients with cervical spine injuries. Fingers and palms of both hands are used to stabilize the patient's occiput and mastoid processes to ensure successful airway intervention.
questions.learning: Head tilt, chin lift — The maneuver being performed in the given image is that of head-tilt chin-lift. It is an important technique in emergency airway management to open up the airway.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young person with recurrent seasonal conjunctivitis presents with itchiness and watering in the eyes. What is the most likely cell involved in the immediate phase of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mast cells

The given clinical features of allergic reactions suggest Type 1 hypersensitivity which is mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) binding to mast cells.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity, also called allergic reactions or allergies is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to an IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It has two phases.

Early phase: The mediators produced by the mast cells are responsible for most of the immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Histamine and leukotrienes are released rapidly from the sensitized mast cells and trigger intense immediate reactions characterized by edema, mucus secretion, and smooth muscle spasm.

Other mediators involved in the early phase are,

* Enzymes: neutral proteases (chymase, tryptase) and acid hydrolases

* Proteoglycans: heparin and chondroitin sulfate

* Lipid mediators: Platelet-activating factor (PAF)

Late-phase: The late-phase reaction is characterized by the recruitment of leukocytes, that amplify and sustain the inflammatory response without exposure to the triggering antigen.

Mediators involved in the late phase of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction are:

* Cytokines: TNF, IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, and chemokines (eotaxin)

* Leukocytes (eosinophils)

* Major Basic Protein (MBP)

* Eosinophil cationic protein

The sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity

Though eosinophils and neutrophils are involved later in the pathogenesis, mast cells are central to the development of immediate hypersensitivity.

Pearl PF0858: Disorders Caused by Immediate Hypersensitivity

Clinical Syndrome

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Anaphylaxis (may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food)

Fall in blood pressure (shock) caused by vascular dilation; airway obstruction due to laryngeal edema

Bronchial asthma

Airway obstruction caused by bronchial smooth muscle hyperactivity; inflammation and tissue injury caused by late-phase reaction

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

Food allergies

Increased peristalsis due to contraction of intestinal muscles
questions.learning: Mast cells — The given clinical features of allergic reactions suggest Type 1 hypersensitivity which is mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) binding to mast cells.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male came with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He has skin lesions that appear as umbilicated papules and nodules predominantly on the face, trunk, and upper extremities. Chest x-ray showed multiple bilateral nodular infiltrates. His sputum CBNAAT for tuberculosis was negative and he has a low CD4 count. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis.

Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) is seen in immunocompromised patients. Common risk factors are AIDS (CD4+ T-cell count, <200/μL), extremes of age, the administration of immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., prednisone, mycophenolate, calcineurin inhibitors), and use of drugs like methotrexate, anti-TNF-α agents, and other biologic response modifiers for autoimmune disorders. It most commonly involves the lungs and bone marrow.

Patients with PDH can present with diffuse interstitial or reticulonodular lung infiltrates that can cause respiratory failure, shock, coagulopathy, and multiorgan failure. Clinical features are fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and thrombocytopenia. They may also present with meningitis or focal brain lesions, ulcerations of the oral mucosa, gastrointestinal ulcerations and bleeding, and adrenal insufficiency.

Cutaneous involvement is noted in about 10% of cases of PDH. Skin lesions can be caused by the fungus itself resulting in the formation of papules, plaques, nodules, or ulcers, or by an immune response to the infection causing erythema nodosum or erythema multiforme.

Laboratory investigations include looking for Histoplasma antigen in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, serum, and urine, IgG and IgM antibodies in serology, a fungal culture of blood or bone marrow aspirate, and cytopathology on biopsy of the affected organ.

Histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum is a thermally dimorphic fungus. The yeast form occurs mainly in tissues at a temperature of 37 °C and the mycelial form occurs in the soil at 25 °C. At room temperature, white, cottony, mycelial growth appears, with large (8-20 μ) thick-walled, spherical spores with tubercles (finger-like projections called tuberculate spores). Transmission is mainly via inhalation of microconidia.

Treatment involves liposomal amphotericin B,  followed by itraconazole for at least 12 months.

Other options:

Option B: If the disease involves skin with signs of meningitis, then HIV with disseminated cryptococcosis can be considered. Since the patient has no signs of meningitis, this option can be ruled out.

Option C: If the disease is restricted to the skin alone, it can be HIV with disseminated molluscum contagiosum. Since the question mentions lung involvement, the option is ruled out.

Option D: The question mentions that CBNAAT for tuberculosis was negative. Hence, this option is ruled out.
questions.learning: HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis — The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis. Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) is seen in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following devices can be used in a patient with bilateral external auditory canal atresia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

Device 1 shown in the above image represents bone anchored hearing aid (BAHA), which can be used in a patient with bilateral external auditory canal atresia. Cochlear implants (Device 2) are primarily used to restore sensorineural hearing loss, whereas BAHA is used in cases with defects in the outer or middle ear.

External auditory canal atresia refers to the absence of a patent ear canal and this can either be congenital or acquired.

Congenital atresia: The external ear develops from the first and second pharyngeal arch and the first pharyngeal cleft. Atresia of the external canal can occur in association with microtia (under-developed pinna) or with abnormalities of the middle ear, internal ear, and other structures. It is usually bilateral.

Acquired atresia: A rare condition, following external ear trauma, such as road traffic accidents, gunshot wounds, or recent otologic surgery. In rare instances, canal stenosis and atresia have been observed in association with neoplastic changes and idiopathic inflammatory processes.

Bilateral aural atresia will present with failed audiological testing and require early bone conduction hearing aids, one of which is BAHA, that combines a sound processor with a small titanium fixture implanted behind the ear and allows the bone to transfer sound to a functioning cochlea rather than via the middle ear – a process known as direct bone conduction.

A picture of BAHA is shown below. It consists of three parts, an innermost titanium fixture in the bone, a middle abutment, and an outer hearing aid fixed to the abutment.

Bone-anchored Hearing Aids (BAHA) are used:

• When air-conduction (AC) hearing aid cannot be used:

• People who have chronic inflammation or infection of the ear canal associated with discharge and cannot wear standard “in the ear” air-conduction hearing aids.
• Children with malformed or absent outer ear and ear canals as in microtia or canal atresia.

• In conductive or mixed hearing loss, e.g. otosclerosis and tympanosclerosis where surgery is contraindicated
• In unilateral deafness

Other options:

Option B: Device 2 is a picture of a cochlear implant. It is a medical device that uses electricity to stimulate the spiral ganglion cells of the auditory nerve to restore sensorineural hearing loss. It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the hearing nerve, which bypasses the damaged hearing apparatus. It cannot be used in patients with cochlear aplasia or without the VIIIth cranial nerve.

Option C: Device 3 is a picture of a stapedectomy piston, used in patients with otosclerosis.

Option D: Device 4 is a picture of a partial ossicular replacement prosthesis that is designed for situations when the incus and/or malleus are eroded but the stapes is structurally intact.
questions.learning: 1 Device 1 shown in the above image represents bone anchored hearing aid (BAHA), which can be used in a patient with bilateral external auditory canal atresia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant presents with bleeding from the umbilical cord. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vit K

Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) is the most common cause of spontaneous bleeding in newborns. Bleeding from the umbilical stump, gastrointestinal tract, skin, or intracranial sites occurs due to deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, and X).

Why are newborns deficient in vitamin K?

• Poor placental transfer of vitamin K
• Sterile intestine (lack of vitamin K-producing gut flora)
• Low vitamin K content in breast milk

Key differentiating features:

• Vitamin K deficiency:

• Umbilical stump bleeding
• Prolonged PT/INR (earliest abnormality)
• May also prolong aPTT in severe deficiency
• Vitamin C deficiency: Gum bleeding, petechiae (older infants/children)
• Hemophilia: Deep tissue/joint bleeding with prolonged aPTT
• Thrombocytopenia: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding with low platelet count
questions.learning: Vit K Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) is the most common cause of spontaneous bleeding in newborns. Bleeding from the umbilical stump, gastrointestinal tract, skin, or intracranial sites occurs due to deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following are considered radioprotectors, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cisplatin

• Radioprotectors are agents that protect normal tissues from radiation-induced damage by scavenging free radicals or enhancing DNA repair.
• Examples: amifostine, melatonin, and zinc compounds which reduce radiation toxicity to healthy cells.
• Cisplatin is not a radioprotector; it is a radiosensitizer that enhances the effect of radiation on tumor cells by increasing DNA damage and inhibiting repair, thereby improving cancer treatment efficacy.
questions.learning: Cisplatin • Radioprotectors are agents that protect normal tissues from radiation-induced damage by scavenging free radicals or enhancing DNA repair. • Examples: amifostine, melatonin, and zinc compounds which reduce radiation toxicity to healthy cells. •…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with low backache and weight loss. He has progressive difficulty in urination and had an episode of urinary retention 2 days back which was relieved by catheterization.PSA was done which was 5.2 ng/ml and an X-Ray LS spine shows osteoblastic changes. What is the clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prostate cancer

The given clinical details with elevated PSA and blastic changes in the LS spine suggest a diagnosis of carcinoma prostate.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumour in men over the age of 65 years. The growth and survival of prostate cancer cells depend on androgens.  Approximately 70% of carcinomas of the prostate arise in the peripheral zone of the gland, classically in a posterior location.

Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Grading of prostate cancer by the modified Gleason system correlates with pathologic stage and prognosis.

Measurement of serum PSA levels is widely used to assist in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of prostate cancer.

Prostatic biopsy specimen showing foci of small crowded glands, some showing cribriform pattern of arrangement.

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma
questions.learning: Prostate cancer — The given clinical details with elevated PSA and blastic changes in the LS spine suggest a diagnosis of carcinoma prostate. Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumour in men over the age of 65 years.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child transfers an object from one hand to another. What does it signify?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ability to compare objects

The milestone of transfer of objects from one hand to another in a child signifies the ability of the child to compare objects. The transfer of objects is a motor milestone occurring at 6 months of age.

Other options:

Option A: When the child reaches for objects it implies the onset of visuomotor coordination. It is attained at 4 months

Option C: Thumb finger grasp implies the ability to handle small objects. It is attained at 8 months.

Option D: The voluntary release/ Release phenomenon is used to denote the disappearance of the palmar grasp, which is seen at 4 months.
questions.learning: Ability to compare objects — The milestone of transfer of objects from one hand to another in a child signifies the ability of the child to compare objects.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about anti-CMV IgG antibodies?
options: Denotes chronic CMV infection with immunity to other serotypes
IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating past and primary infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating past and primary infection

IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating past and primary infection with cytomegalovirus (CMV).

Avidity level measured by avidity index is used to describe the percentage of IgG bound to the antigen after being treated with denaturing agents.These assays are based on the fact that low avidity IgG antibodies are present during the first few months after the infection and avidity increases over time indicating maturation of the immune response. So the presence of high avidity IgG denotes a past infection rather than a primary one. Low avidity IgG signals a primary infection within the last 3-4 months.

IgM detection can be used as an indicator of acute infection, but it lacks specificity for primary infection. This is because it persists for years in some individuals and is also produced during reactivation.

Cytomegalovirus is a type of herpes virus, which causes severe disease in immunocompromised patients. In most other cases, it is inapparent and marked by prolonged latency with intermittent reactivation.
questions.learning: IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating past and primary infection IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating past and primary infection with cytomegalovirus (CMV).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The biochemical form of amyloid in haemodialysis associated amylodosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aβ2m

Patients on long-term hemodialysis for renal failure can develop amyloidosis as a result of the deposition of β2-microglobulin leading to major fibril protein Aβ2m.

This protein is present in high concentrations in the serum of persons with renal disease.Patients sometimes presented with carpal tunnel syndrome because of β2-microglobulin deposition.

Amyloidosis is a condition caused due to the deposition of abnormal fibrillar proteins in extracellular spaces. Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, and plasma proteins, notably serum amyloid P component (SAP). Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

Based on the involvement of organ systems it may be classified as systemic or localized. A hereditary amyloidosis is a separate group of heterogeneous disorders with many distinctive patterns of organ involvement.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blood volume control by kidney

In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity could be seen in blood volume control by the kidney.

When the blood volume falls below the equilibrium, the renal–body fluid mechanism causes the blood volume returns back to the equilibrium point resulting in zero error and hence the gain of kidney in its ability to regulate blood volume is infinity (∞).

The degree of effectiveness with which a regulatory system maintains constant conditions is determined by the gain of the negative feedback system.

Gain= Correction/Error

Example: If an external or internal factor led to a decrease in mean blood pressure from 100 mm Hg to 80 mm Hg. Activation of a negative feedback mechanism i.e. baroreflex leads to a correction of blood pressure to 96 mm Hg. So in this case,

• Correction = 16 mm Hg
• Error = 4 mm Hg
• Gain = Correction/Error = 16/4 = 4

Note: A gain of 0 would imply a total failure of the regulatory system and a gain of infinity (∞) would indicate complete restoration of the regulated variable.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which condition is characterized by the presence of an empty delta sign on imaging?
questions.explanation: The "empty delta sign" is the pathognomonic radiological finding for Cerebral Venous (Sinus) Thrombosis on a contrast-enhanced CT scan. It refers to a triangular area of non-enhancement (the thrombus) surrounded by the enhancing wall of the superior sagittal sinus. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A) presents with blood in the sulci and cisterns. Subdural hemorrhage (Option B) is a crescentic blood collection, and Intra parenchymal hemorrhage (Option D) is blood within the brain tissue. Cerebral venous thrombosis is a common cause of stroke in young adults, particularly women (associated with pregnancy, oral contraceptives, or dehydration). Patients typically present with headache, seizures, and focal deficits. While the empty delta sign is specific, the gold standard for diagnosis is MR venography (MRV). Prompt treatment with anticoagulation (even in the presence of venous hemorrhage) is essential to prevent venous infarction and improve neurological outcomes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presents with gradual painless decrease in vision. Fundus examination shows macular edema. He is planned for an intravitreal sustained-release steroid implant that is FDA approved for this condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexamethasone 0.7 mg

Ozurdex (dexamethasone intravitreal implant 0.7 mg) is the biodegradable sustained-release implant (NOVADUR polymer matrix) approved for:

• Diabetic macular edema
• Macular edema following CRVO/BRVO
• Non-infectious posterior uveitis

Why the distractors are wrong?

• A. Betamethasone (0.6%) — not used as an intravitreal implant; irrelevant to posterior segment sustained delivery.
• C./D. Triamcinolone acetonide (0.5%/0.4 mg or 0.7%) — intravitreal triamcinolone is used off-label/approved in some contexts, but it's a suspension/crystalline steroid, not a sustained-release biodegradable implant. There's no FDA-approved "triamcinolone 0.7% implant" — this option is a distractor mixing up drug and implant nomenclature.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which form of vitiligo is initially progressive and later becomes stable and non-progressive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Segmental

Segmental vitiligo is characterized by an initial rapid progression followed by long-term stability.

• Pattern: Unilateral, dermatomal/segmental distribution
• Course:

o    Early phase → rapid spread

o    Later → stabilizes and becomes non-progressive

• Onset: Usually earlier age than other types
• Response to therapy: Often less responsive to medical therapy, better suited for surgical treatments (grafting) once stable

Contrast with other types:

• Non-segmental vitiligo (acrofacial, generalized, mixed) → chronic, relapsing, unpredictable course
• Focal vitiligo → localized but may progress or evolve

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the conversion of T4 to T3, in the peripheral tissue?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iodothyronine deiodinase I

Peripheral T3 conversion from T4 is catalyzed by the enzyme iodothryronine deiodinase I. T4 undergoes deiodination in extrathyroidal tissue to form T3, which is the active form of the hormone. It is expressed predominantly in the peripheral tissues.

Iodothyronine deiodinase II: Iodothyronine deiodinase type II (DIO2) is an enzyme responsible for the activation of T4 to T3 in certain specific tissues, such as the hypothalamus and pituitary gland.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with a swelling over the wrist that varies in size, associated with mild hand numbness and occasional pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a wrist swelling that fluctuates in size and causes occasional pain or numbness is highly characteristic of a ganglion cyst. These are benign, fluid-filled sacs that typically arise from joint capsules or tendon sheaths, most commonly on the dorsal aspect of the wrist. Numbness may occur if the cyst compresses an adjacent nerve. A lipoma (Option A) is a soft, fatty mass that does not typically fluctuate in size or arise directly from joint structures. A dermoid cyst (Option C) is usually congenital, midline, and contains ectodermal elements like hair or sebum. A hematoma (Option D) follows acute trauma and presents with bruising and initial pain that subsides as it resolves. Diagnosis of a ganglion is confirmed by its translucent nature on transillumination and clinical location
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a wrist swelling that fluctuates in size and causes occasional pain or numbness is highly characteristic of a ganglion cyst.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with diarrhea, cognitive impairment, and a characteristic rash. Which vitamin deficiency most likely explains these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with the "3 Ds" of pellagra: Diarrhea, Dermatitis (distinctive rash), and Dementia (memory impairment). Pellagra is the clinical result of Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency (Option B). The rash in pellagra is typically symmetrical and appears on sun-exposed areas, classically forming a "necklace" pattern around the neck known as Casal's necklace. Niacin is essential for the production of NAD and NADP, which are vital coenzymes for energy metabolism. Thiamine deficiency (Option A) leads to Beriberi or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Cyanocobalamin (B12) deficiency (Option C) causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological degeneration. Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) deficiency (Option D) leads to scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Pellagra can be caused by a diet based primarily on corn, which is low in available niacin and its precursor tryptophan. Thus, Niacin is the responsible vitamin
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with the "3 Ds" of pellagra: Diarrhea, Dermatitis (distinctive rash), and Dementia (memory impairment). Pellagra is the clinical result of Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency (Option B).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is false about Anatomy of Adrenal gland?
options: Adrenals are yellow in gross appearance
Right adrenal is semilunar in shape
Left adrenal is related medially to coeliac ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right adrenal is semilunar in shape

The adrenal (suprarenal) glands are paired endocrine glands located in the retroperitoneum on the superior poles of the kidneys.

• Color: Adrenal glands appear yellowish due to their high lipid content, especially in the cortex.
• Location: They are retroperitoneal structures situated within the renal fascia above the kidneys.
• Shape difference:

• Right adrenal gland → Pyramidal/triangular in shape.
• Left adrenal gland → Semilunar (crescentic) in shape.

Important Relations:

• The left adrenal gland is medially related to the coeliac ganglion and coeliac trunk.
• The right adrenal gland is related anteriorly to the inferior vena cava and liver.

Option C states that the right adrenal is semilunar, which is incorrect. The semilunar shape belongs to the left adrenal gland, while the right adrenal gland is pyramidal.
