questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 22-year-old college student presents with multiple small depigmented skin lesions that have been present for over two years, as shown in the accompanying image. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vitiligo is a common acquired chronic depigmenting disorder characterized by the loss of functional melanocytes from the epidermis. This results in the "milky-white," well-demarcated macules and patches seen in the image. It often affects the hands, face, and genital areas. Melasma (Option A) presents as hyperpigmented (dark) brown patches, typically on the face, and is related to hormonal changes or UV exposure. Psoriasis (Option C) features erythematous plaques with silvery scales, not depigmentation. Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option D) presents with intensely itchy, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, often associated with celiac disease. Vitiligo can have a significant psychological impact on young adults like this college student. Diagnosis is clinical, though Wood’s lamp examination can help highlight the areas of depigmentation. Management options include topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and phototherapy (NB-UVB), aimed at inducing repigmentation and stabilizing the disease
questions.learning: Vitiligo is a common acquired chronic depigmenting disorder characterized by the loss of functional melanocytes from the epidermis. This results in the "milky-white," well-demarcated macules and patches seen in the image.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following findings are seen in Diabetic Retinopathy on fundus examination? 1. Microaneurysm 2. Dot and blot hemorrhage 3. Retinal thickening 4. Neovascularization Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus and a leading cause of preventable blindness. Fundus examination reveals characteristic retinal vascular changes, beginning with microaneurysms and progressing to hemorrhages, exudates, and neovascularization in advanced disease.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Microaneurysm✅: Earliest clinically detectable sign of diabetic retinopathy.
• 2. Dot and blot hemorrhage✅: Characteristic of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR).
• 4. Neovascularization✅: Hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Retinal thickening❌: Indicates diabetic macular edema (DME) rather than being a characteristic feature used to classify diabetic retinopathy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the causative organism of angular conjunctivitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Moraxella lacunata

Moraxella species, a type of gram-negative diplobacilli, are involved in causing angular conjunctivitis which is a type of chronic conjunctivitis.

Angular conjunctivitis is a chronic type of conjunctivitis where there is inflammation of the conjunctiva at the lid margins and the inner and outer canthi of the eyes with red, scaly, excoriated, macerated and fissured skin at the canthi. This is because of the proteolytic enzymes secreted by the Moraxella species.

Patients with angular conjunctivitis usually experience eye irritation, a burning sensation and collection of dirty-white, foamy discharge at the angles. These patients can also have associated blepharitis and papillary and follicular conjunctivitis.

Causative organisms are Moraxella lacunata, Moraxella axenfeld and Staphylococcus aureus (Rare cause). The source of infection is typically the nasal tract or the nasal discharge of patients with angular conjunctivitis. The infection spreads from the nasal cavity to the eyes through contaminated hands or handkerchiefs. Treatment includes oxytetracycline 1% ointment for 10 to 14 days, and zinc oxide as it inhibits proteolytic enzymes.

The image given below shows the eye of a patient infected with angular conjunctivitis.

Other options:

Option B: Haemophilus influenzae causes acute conjunctivitis.

Option C: Adenovirus is the most common cause of viral conjunctivitis and it most commonly causes follicular conjunctivitis, pharyngoconjunctival fever, and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.

Option D: Coxsackie B virus is known to cause aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, pericarditis, and myocarditis. There are no known mentions of ocular disease caused by the virus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A long-term study observed that individuals with high blood pressure in childhood tended to have high blood pressure in adulthood, while those with low childhood blood pressure generally maintained lower levels later in life. Which epidemiological concept does this pattern best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Tracking of blood pressure refers to the epidemiological phenomenon where an individual's relative position or "rank" within a population distribution remains consistent over time. For example, a child whose BP is at the 90th percentile for their age is statistically likely to remain at the high end of the BP distribution as an adult. This concept is vital for identifying future cardiovascular risk and implementing early prevention. The Rule of Halves (Option A) relates to the under-diagnosis and under-treatment of hypertension in a community. Regression to the mean (Option B) is a statistical concept where extreme measurements tend to move closer to the average upon repeat testing. A cohort effect (Option D) refers to shared characteristics or outcomes in a group based on their time of birth or shared experiences. Only "tracking" accurately describes the lifelong persistence of BP status
questions.learning: Tracking of blood pressure refers to the epidemiological phenomenon where an individual's relative position or "rank" within a population distribution remains consistent over time.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in osteoporosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Normal calcium and normal ALP

Osteoporosis is associated with normal calcium, normal ALP levels and phosphorous.

Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

Risk factors for osteoporosis include:

• Increasing age
• Female sex
• Alcohol
• Smoking
• Previous history of fragility fractures
• Family history of hip fracture
• Low body mass index- less than 18.5 kg/m2
• Excessive usage of glucocorticoids
• They present with fractures that occur without any trauma or as a result of low-impact trauma. The commonly associated fractures are fractures of the distal part of the radius (Colle's fracture), fractures of the hip, and fractures of the vertebrae. In severe cases, the fracture of vertebrae can cause kyphosis.

Radiological findings:

• A decreased vertical height of the vertebra due to collapse
• Ground glass appearance - especially in bones like pelvis
• Codfish appearance - it occurs due to bulging of the disc into the adjacent vertebral bodies so that it becomes biconcave

DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. T-score less than -2.5 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip indicates osteoporosis.

Treatment - the mainstay is to reduce the risk of fractures. Following medications can be useful:

• Bisphosphonates. They are the first line of medication. They reduce osteoclastic bone resorption and prevent bone loss. Eg. zoledronate
• Denosumab- This is an antibody to the RANK ligand. It prevents the activation of RANK which is required for the proliferation of osteoclasts. Therefore, it decreases bone resorption
• Parathyroid hormone - Preotact and teriparatide are recombinant parathyroid hormone analogues. At low and intermittent doses, they can promote bone formation.
• Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs)- They act on the estrogen receptors and prevent bone resorption. Eg. raloxifene.
• Strontium ranelate- It is thought to increase bone formation and reduce bone resorption.
• Cathepsin K inhibitor- inhibits the activity of collagenases (eg, odanacatib)
• Sclerostin inhibitor- Sclerostin inhibits the activity of osteoblasts. Romosozumab is a humanized antisclerostin monoclonal antibody that increases bone formation.

Operative treatment is required for femoral neck and other long bone fractures.
questions.learning: Normal calcium and normal ALP Osteoporosis is associated with normal calcium, normal ALP levels and phosphorous. Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following is due to the deficiency of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A

The given image depicts Bitot's spots characteristically seen in deficiency of vitamin A. Bitot's spots are seen as white patches of keratinized epithelium on the sclera. It is more commonly bilateral and on the temporal side.

Vitamin A deficiency arises mostly due to the inadequate amounts of vitamin A in diet. It can present as night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. In later stages, it can lead to xerophthalmia. It also increases the risk of developing measles, diarrhea, and dysentery. Skin manifestations include xerosis, scaling, and dermomalacia. Phrynoderma may also be seen as keratotic follicular papules affecting the thighs and upper arms. It is shown in the image below.

In patients above the age of 1 year, vitamin A deficiency is treated with 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular route. It should be repeated the next day and two weeks later.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that plays an essential role in vision, reproduction, and maintenance of epithelial integrity. The various forms of vitamin A include retinol (storage form), retinal, retinoic acid, and beta-carotene. It is stored in the liver perisinusoidal stellate (Ito) cells as retinyl ester (retinyl palmitate).

Other options:

Option A - Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin that aids in iron absorption and collagen maturation. It cannot be synthesized in humans because of the absence of L-gulonolactone oxidase. Vitamin C deficiency results in scurvy.

Option C - Vitamin B deficiency has clinical manifestations pertaining to each type.

Option D - Vitamin E deficiency can present as posterior column and spinocerebellar symptoms. Peripheral neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, and pigmented retinopathy are other features seen.
questions.learning: Vitamin — A The given image depicts Bitot's spots characteristically seen in deficiency of vitamin A. Bitot's spots are seen as white patches of keratinized epithelium on the sclera.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An HIV-positive man presents with a high-grade fever. Examination reveals a positive Kernig's sign. CSF shows reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes. A diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Liposomal amphotericin B+ flucytosine

The appropriate management in this patient of cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B (LAMB)+ flucytosine

Cryptococcus is the leading infectious cause of meningitis in patients with AIDS. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL. Most patients present with a picture of subacute meningoencephalitis. The CSF profile may show modest elevations in WBC or protein levels and a decrease in glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated (yeast colonies obstruct the free flow of CSF causing increased CSF pressure).

The diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made by the identification of Cryptococcus neoformans yeast cells in CSF with India ink stain or by the detection of cryptococcal antigen using latex agglutination (CrAg).

Prophylaxis: Oral fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.

Treatment:

* Induction - Liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative.

* Maintenance - Oral fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART.

Other Options:

Option A: Vancomycin would be appropriate for bacterial meningitis caused by organisms like Streptococcus pneumoniae or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Option B: High dose fluconazole with flucytosine is used in cryptococcal meningitis, but they are not the first-line therapy for the induction phase. Fluconazole with flucytosine is typically used in the consolidation phase after initial treatment with amphotericin B, or in resource-limited settings where amphotericin B is not available.

Option C: Voriconazole while effective against many fungi, is not the drug of choice for cryptococcal meningitis. It's primarily indicated for invasive aspergillosis and other specific fungal infections.
questions.learning: Liposomal amphotericin B+ flucytosine — The appropriate management in this patient of cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B (LAMB)+ flucytosine Cryptococcus is the leading infectious cause of meningitis in patients with AIDS.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with long-standing, recurrent watery diarrhea that is refractory to conventional treatment, along with weakness, dehydration, and hypokalemia. Blood tests reveal markedly elevated levels of a specific peptide. Based on these findings, which pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of profuse, chronic, watery diarrhea, dehydration, and hypokalemia is characteristic of "pancreatic cholera," also known as Verner-Morrison syndrome. This syndrome is caused by a VIPoma, a neuroendocrine tumor (usually in the pancreas) that secretes excessive Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP). VIP stimulates intestinal secretion and inhibits gastric acid, resulting in the WDHA syndrome (Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria). Glucagonoma (Option B) presents with necrolytic migratory erythema and mild diabetes. Insulinoma (Option C) causes hypoglycemia. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (Option D) is caused by a gastrinoma, resulting in severe peptic ulcers rather than the painless, watery "cholera-like" diarrhea seen here. Therefore, because the specific biochemical triad of watery diarrhea and low potassium is linked to VIP overproduction, VIPoma is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of profuse, chronic, watery diarrhea, dehydration, and hypokalemia is characteristic of "pancreatic cholera," also known as Verner-Morrison syndrome.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In cases of alcohol abuse, which substance is typically used to preserve blood samples during autopsy for alcohol analysis?
questions.explanation: This forensic principle, as discussed in Question 64, is essential for maintaining the validity of post-mortem blood alcohol testing. During an autopsy, sodium fluoride is used to preserve the blood sample. It functions as a potent preservative and enzyme inhibitor that prevents the post-mortem production of alcohol by bacteria and yeast. Without sodium fluoride, microorganisms could ferment the glucose naturally present in the body, leading to a "false positive" or an artificially high alcohol reading that does not reflect the patient's state before death. Formalin (Option B) is used to preserve tissue for histology but would interfere with chemical testing. Rectified spirit (Option C) is concentrated ethanol and would obviously invalidate any alcohol measurement. Sodium chloride (Option D) is simple table salt and lacks the necessary enzymatic-inhibitory properties. In a medico-legal context, the use of sodium fluoride-preserved tubes is a mandatory step to ensure that the chemical evidence presented in court is scientifically robust
questions.learning: This forensic principle, as discussed in Question 64, is essential for maintaining the validity of post-mortem blood alcohol testing. During an autopsy, sodium fluoride is used to preserve the blood sample.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ritodrine is a medication primarily used to prevent premature labor. Which of the following is NOT a typical maternal complication associated with its use?
questions.explanation: Ritodrine is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist used as a tocolytic to suppress uterine contractions in preterm labor. Due to its systemic beta-adrenergic effects, it is associated with several well-known maternal complications. These include fine skeletal muscle tremors (Option A), significant tachycardia and palpitations (Option B), and potentially life-threatening pulmonary edema (Option D), especially when used with corticosteroids or excessive IV fluids. Notably, the metabolic effect of ritodrine is to increase blood sugar levels through glycogenolysis; therefore, it causes hyperglycemia, NOT hypoglycemia (Option C). Hypoglycemia is the correct "NOT" choice as it is the opposite of the expected physiological response to beta-agonists. Clinicians must carefully monitor maternal pulse, lung sounds, and glucose levels during ritodrine administration to ensure patient safety. Thus, hyperglycemia is the standard metabolic side effect of this medication
questions.learning: Ritodrine is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist used as a tocolytic to suppress uterine contractions in preterm labor. Due to its systemic beta-adrenergic effects, it is associated with several well-known maternal complications.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Based on the disease shown in the image, which of the following specimens would the filarial worms be absent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saliva

The image is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis, and the filarial worms cannot be demonstrated in saliva.

Lymphatic filariasis occurs due to the transmission of W.bancrofti by the bite of Culex mosquitoes. The third stage larval forms from the mosquito enter the lymphatics and lymph nodes where they develop into adult worms. The adult worms become sexually mature and mate to release microfilariae which enter the peripheral circulation.

The disease initially causes acute attacks of lymphangitis and lymphadenitis. Early treatment may even cure the disease. The lymphedema may gradually worsen and get associated with the thickening of the skin and fibrosis of lymph vessels or blockage by adult worms. Hydrocele is another common manifestation that occurs due to lymphatic obstruction.

Microfilaria can be demonstrated in blood, chylous urine, exudate of lymph varix, and hydrocele fluid, however, peripheral blood is the preferred choice. The examination of a thick and thin blood smear stained with Giemsa stain shows the microfilaria. Other methods are by examining the unstained blood under a microscope for the actively motile microfilariae and by acridine orange-microhematocrit tube technique.

The best time to collect the blood samples is at night, between 10 pm and 4 am as they are nocturnally periodic.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

The image below shows the life cycle of Wuchereria bancrofti.

*Note:

* W.bancrofti causes Bancroftian filariasis and is transmitted by Culex quinquefasciatus (C. fatigans). In India, Wuchereria bancrofti is the commonest cause of filariasis.

* B. malayi causes Burgian filariasis and the vector is the Mansonia mosquito.

Pearl PF1933: Filarial worms and their morphology
questions.learning: Saliva — The image is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis, and the filarial worms cannot be demonstrated in saliva. Lymphatic filariasis occurs due to the transmission of W.bancrofti by the bite of Culex mosquitoes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the fracture site in the X-ray shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6th and 7th rib

The given X-ray shows the fracture of the 6th and 7th rib

In the chest X-ray, ribs appear as light grey strips. The anterior part of the rib is more oblique and the medial part cannot be demonstrable as it ends with costal cartilage. The posterior part of the rib is more horizontal and the attachment of the rib with the vertebra can be easily made out.

Normal Chest X-ray Rib Identification

The anterior(yellow) and posterior(red) ribs are highlighted in the image given below.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The following image is of the most common cause of stridor in children. Identify it.
questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx and the most frequent cause of inspiratory stridor in infants. It is characterized by "floppiness" of the supraglottic tissues, which collapse into the airway during inspiration. The endoscopic image shows the classic triad: an omega-shaped (tightly folded) epiglottis, short and thickened aryepiglottic folds, and bulky arytenoid mucosa. The stridor typically worsens when the infant is supine or crying and improves when prone. Option B (Laryngeal papilloma) would show warty, cauliflower-like growths on the vocal cords. Option C (Chronic epiglottitis) is rare in children and would show diffuse thickening. Option D (Laryngocele) is an air-filled sac communicating with the saccule. Most cases of laryngomalacia are self-limiting and resolve by age 18–24 months as the cartilages mature. However, severe cases causing failure to thrive, hypoxia, or sleep apnea may require surgical intervention, such as a supraglottoplasty
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx and the most frequent cause of inspiratory stridor in infants. It is characterized by "floppiness" of the supraglottic tissues, which collapse into the airway during inspiration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the aetiological factors associated with a communicating hydrocephalus? I. Post haemorrhagic II. Lesions within the ventricle III. CSF infection IV. Raised CSF protein Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when there is impaired absorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at the arachnoid villi (granulations) despite patent ventricular pathways. Since the ventricular system communicates freely with the subarachnoid space, all ventricles enlarge uniformly.

The following conditions cause communicating hydrocephalus:

• I. Post-haemorrhagic: Subarachnoid or intraventricular hemorrhage causes blood products to obstruct the arachnoid granulations, reducing CSF absorption.
• III. CSF infection: Meningitis causes inflammation and fibrosis of the arachnoid villi, impairing CSF absorption.
• IV. Raised CSF protein: High CSF protein (e.g., in Guillain-Barré syndrome, spinal tumors, chronic meningitis) increases CSF viscosity and interferes with absorption.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Lesions within the ventricle: Intraventricular lesions (e.g., colloid cyst, intraventricular tumor) obstruct CSF flow and cause non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus, not communicating hydrocephalus.
questions.learning: I, III and IV Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when there is impaired absorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at the arachnoid villi (granulations) despite patent ventricular pathways.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with both the "lemon sign" and "spina bifida" on a prenatal ultrasound?
questions.explanation: The "lemon sign" refers to the inward scalloping of the frontal bones on an axial prenatal ultrasound of the fetal skull, giving it a shape resembling a lemon. This sign is a highly sensitive secondary marker for open Neural Tube Defects (NTDs), specifically spina bifida. It occurs because the spinal defect leads to a drop in cerebrospinal fluid pressure, causing the brain to shift caudally (Arnold-Chiari II malformation) and the skull to deform. Anencephaly (Option B) is an NTD where the skull vault and brain are largely absent, so a lemon sign cannot be seen. Down Syndrome (Option C) is associated with markers like increased nuchal translucency or a "double bubble" sign, not the lemon sign. Brachycephaly (Option D) refers to a broad, short skull shape seen in various syndromes or as a normal variant, but not specifically linked to spinal lesions. Therefore, the lemon sign is a classic sonographic indicator for identifying occult or overt spina bifida
questions.learning: The "lemon sign" refers to the inward scalloping of the frontal bones on an axial prenatal ultrasound of the fetal skull, giving it a shape resembling a lemon.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase

Methotrexate is an antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue that inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Methotrexate and its polyglutamate also inhibit the enzymes involved in de novo purine and thymidylate synthesis.

It is curative in choriocarcinoma and is used to maintain remission in children with acute leukemias. It has prominent immunosuppressant properties that are useful in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and many other autoimmune disorders. When toxicity occurs, it manifests as nausea, loose stool, stomatitis, punctate cutaneous eruption, alopecia and hematologic abnormalities, particularly macrocytosis.

Pearl PF1704: Classification of antineoplastic drugs
questions.learning: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase Methotrexate is an antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue that inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient with a known case of chronic plaque psoriasis with more than 50% skin involvement presents to you. Which of the following will you not recommend?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral steroids

Oral/systemic steroids are not used in the management of chronic plaque psoriasis. Topical steroids may be used.

Systemic steroids are avoided because the withdrawal of systemic steroids causes the development of pustular psoriasis.

The only indication of using systemic steroids in psoriasis is generalized pustular psoriasis in pregnancy (impetigo herpetiformis).

Other options maybe used in treatment of extensive (>30%) chronic plaque psoriasis.
questions.learning: Oral steroids Oral/systemic steroids are not used in the management of chronic plaque psoriasis. Systemic steroids are avoided because the withdrawal of systemic steroids causes the development of pustular psoriasis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 20-year-old female presents with irregular periods. Her ultrasound scan revealed the finding shown in the image. This is most likely due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PCOD

The given ultrasound shows multiple ovarian follicles arranged in a necklace pattern, which is a feature of polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD).

USG Criteria for PCOD-  Either one of the ovaries with:

* Increased ovarian stroma

* 12 follicles, each measuring 2 to 9 mm arranged in a necklace pattern

* Ovarian volume >10 ml

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the anaplerotic reaction among the following?
options: Conversion of pyruvate to Acetyl CoA
Conversion of pyruvate to Lactic acid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conversion of pyruvate to Oxaloacetate

The conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is an anaplerotic reaction. It is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

Anaplerotic reactions are chemical reactions that form intermediates of a metabolic pathway. The above reaction is important in maintaining an adequate concentration of oxaloacetate for the condensation reaction with acetyl-CoA. If acetyl-CoA accumulates, it acts as an activator of pyruvate carboxylase and an inhibitor of pyruvate dehydrogenase, thereby ensuring an adequate supply of oxaloacetate.

Other anaplerotic reactions are:

• Compounds that are metabolized to yield propionyl CoA, which can be then carboxylated and isomerized to succinyl CoA.
• Glutamate and glutamine are important anaplerotic substrates because they yield α-ketoglutarate as a result of the reactions catalyzed by glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase.
• Transamination of aspartate leads directly to the formation of oxaloacetate.
questions.learning: Conversion of pyruvate to Oxaloacetate — The conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is an anaplerotic reaction. It is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the type of transport across the cell membrane given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facilitated diffusion

The given image shows the transport of a molecule across a membrane with the help of a carrier protein. This form of transport is called facilitated diffusion.

When carrier proteins help in the movement of substances in the direction of their chemical or electrical gradients (downhill movement), no energy input is required and the process is called facilitated diffusion.

Glucose transporters or GLUTs are examples of transport proteins in the cell membrane responsible for the transfer of glucose into the cells by facilitated diffusion. Facilitated diffusion involves the passage of molecules or ions inside the cell membrane by binding to a carrier/ transport protein.

Other options -

Option A. Simple diffusion - It is along the concentration gradient but is not carrier-mediated. In the cell, examples of molecules that can use simple diffusion to travel in and out of the cell membrane are water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen. They pass directly through the cell membrane along the concentration gradient, without the use of energy.

Option C. Primary active transport - It is a form of cellular transport requiring energy in the form of hydrolysis of ATP to ship and transfer molecules against gradient differences. The important examples of primary active transport include sodium-potassium ATPase, proton pump, and calcium ATPase.

Option D. Secondary active transport - In this form of transport, two or more substances are transported together across the membrane with help of a carrier molecule. As one of the substances (e.g., sodium) diffuses down its electrochemical gradient, the energy released is used to drive another substance (e.g., glucose) against the gradient. It does not require energy directly from ATP.
questions.learning: Facilitated diffusion — The given image shows the transport of a molecule across a membrane with the help of a carrier protein. This form of transport is called facilitated diffusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presents with hematuria and a neovascular mass in bilateral kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypo-attenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected and produces an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

* Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)

* Absence of ossification or calcification

* The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.

* Approximately 5% may be fat-poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

* Fat-saturated techniques

* Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifacts at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing a 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and an 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following milestones in an infant is achieved at the earliest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ulnar palmar grasp

The milestone which is achieved earliest in the above options is ulnar palmar grasp which is seen by 6 months of age.

Developmental progression of the grasp:

* At 6 months, the infant reaches and holds a larger object in a crude manner using the ulnar aspect of his hand-ulnar palmar grasp.

* At 8-9 months, the object is grasped by the radial side of the palm-radial palmar grasp.

* At 9 months, the immature pincer grasp develops. The object is secured between the adducted thumb and the extended index finger.

* At 12 months, the mature pincer grasp develops. The object is secured between the opposed thumb and the tip of the index finger.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A farmer presented with loose stools and rashes over the sun-exposed areas. Careful diet history reveals a diet rich in maize. Which of the following deficiencies would you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

History of a maize-rich diet along with loose stools and rashes over the sun-exposed areas is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which is low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds- nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes NAD ( nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency

Other options:

Option B: Dietary pyridoxine deficiency (vitamin B6) is rare but has been observed in alcoholics, newborn infants formulas low in vitamin B6, and women taking oral contraceptives. Isoniazid, an anti-TB drug, leads to pyridoxine deficiency resulting in peripheral neuropathy. Hence pyridoxine supplementation is included in ATT regimens.

Option C: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) can manifest as wet beriberi (CVS features like heart failure and edema) or Shoshin beriberi, an acute and fulminant form of wet beriberi, dry beriberi (peripheral neuritis), or as Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis (in alcoholics). Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis.

Option D: Dietary biotin deficiency is unknown but rarely, dermatitis, glossitis, loss of appetite, and nausea may occur after consumption of large amounts of uncooked egg white, which contains the protein avidin. It binds biotin and makes it unavailable for absorption.

Note: A similar image-based question on vitamin B3 deficiency was previously asked in NEET PG 2020. Vitamin deficiencies are a high-yield topic and are repeatedly tested every year.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of alteplase, a tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)?
questions.explanation: Alteplase is a recombinant form of the endogenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). Its primary mechanism of action is to promote fibrinolysis (clot dissolution). It works by binding to fibrin within a thrombus and converting trapped plasminogen into its active form, plasmin. Plasmin then enzymatically breaks down the fibrin meshwork, resulting in the dissolution of the clot. Vitamin K inhibition (Option A) is the mechanism of anticoagulants like warfarin. Factor X inhibition (Option B) is the mechanism of drugs like rivaroxaban or fondaparinux. Activation of thrombin (Option D) would promote clotting, which is the opposite effect of tPA. Alteplase is used as a "clot-buster" in time-sensitive emergencies such as acute ischemic stroke, ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and massive pulmonary embolism. Therefore, its role as a powerful fibrinolytic agent is its definitive pharmacological classification
questions.learning: Alteplase is a recombinant form of the endogenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). Its primary mechanism of action is to promote fibrinolysis (clot dissolution).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypertension is being treated with thiazide diuretics and now complains of fatigue. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypokalemia. Which of the following drugs can be used to prevent potassium loss in this patient?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hypokalemia (low potassium) because they increase the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule, which triggers the secretion of potassium into the urine. To prevent potassium loss while maintaining diuresis, a potassium-sparing diuretic can be added. Amiloride works by directly blocking the Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC) in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, which reduces the driving force for potassium secretion. Furosemide (Option A) is a loop diuretic that causes even more profound potassium loss than thiazides. Acetazolamide (Option C) works in the proximal tubule and also leads to hypokalemia. Indapamide (Option D) is a thiazide-like diuretic that, similar to thiazides, causes potassium depletion. Amiloride is often used in combination with thiazides (e.g., Co-amilozide) to help maintain serum potassium levels within the normal range, preventing the fatigue and arrhythmias associated with hypokalemia
questions.learning: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hypokalemia (low potassium) because they increase the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule, which triggers the secretion of potassium into the urine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Researchers plan to study the relationship between maternal smoking during pregnancy, reported at antenatal visits, and newborn birth weight recorded immediately after delivery. Which study design is most suitable for analyzing this association?
questions.explanation: A prospective cohort study is the most appropriate design because the researchers start with a defined exposure (maternal smoking status reported during antenatal visits) and follow the participants forward in time to observe the outcome (birth weight recorded at delivery). This design allows for the direct calculation of incidence and establishes a clear temporal relationship between exposure and outcome. A retrospective cohort (Option B) would involve looking back at historical records for both exposure and outcome, which is not the case here as the data is collected sequentially. A case-control study (Option C) would start with the outcome (e.g., low birth weight infants) and look backward to find exposures, which is less efficient for a common exposure like smoking. A cross-sectional study (Option D) measures exposure and outcome at a single point in time, failing to provide temporal evidence. Therefore, the longitudinal nature of tracking the pregnancy from early visits to birth identifies this specifically as a prospective cohort study

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following pathogens is correctly matched with its intrinsic drug resistance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Candida krusei - Fluconazole

Among the given options, Candida krusei shows an intrinsic resistance to fluconazole.
The primary or intrinsic resistance of C. krusei to azoles (fluconazole and itraconazole) is mediated through reduced susceptibility of the target enzyme (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) to inhibition by these drugs. However, improved susceptibility is seen with newer generation azoles such as voriconazole.

Life-threatening systemic infections caused by Candida and Aspergillus species are usually seen in severely ill and immunocompromised patients such as HIV, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, and transplant recipients on immunosuppressants. C. albicans and C. dubliniensis are most susceptible to currently available azoles, C. glabrata is less susceptible, whereas C. krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole. Resistance occurs due to overexpression or point mutation in the gene encoding the target enzyme lanosterol 14α-demethylase. Voriconazole is the preferred therapy for multi-drug resistant infection with C. krusei.

C. albicans and C. glabrata (Option C) showing resistance to Amphotericin B has been increasingly reported over the past several years. But this is a secondary resistance due to alteration or a decrease in the amount of ergosterol in the cell membrane. Amphotericin B is indicated to treat C. glabrata that has developed resistance to azoles.

Aspergillus fumigatus, the most common species to cause Aspergillus infection worldwide, also shows an intrinsic resistance to fluconazole. It is susceptible to echinocandins like micafungin, which acts by inhibiting beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, an enzyme necessary for the synthesis of the cell wall.

Other options
Option A : Aspergillus niger is a common cause of otomycosis and is susceptible to azoles like voriconazole, amphotericin B, and echinocandins.
Option D : The drug of choice for treatment of sporotrichosis is itraconazole.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following crystalloid infusions, when given in large quantities, is likely to cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NS

Large-volume infusion of normal saline (0.9% NaCl) delivers excess chloride relative to sodium. Large-volume normal saline → ↑Cl⁻ → ↓HCO₃⁻ → hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap)

This increases plasma chloride, causing bicarbonate dilution and a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.

| Fluid | Key Composition | Effect on Acid-Base

| ----- | --------------- | -------------------

| NS (0.9%) | High Cl⁻ | Causes acidosis

| Ringer Lactate | Lactate → HCO₃⁻ | Alkalinizing

| D5W | Free water | Neutral

| DNS | Dextrose + NS | Mild acidosis possible but less prominent

Ringer lactate is balanced, D5W is free water, and DNS does not cause significant hyperchloremia.
