questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In psychiatry, it is important to differentiate between different types of perceptual disturbances, particularly true hallucinations and pseudohallucinations. Pseudohallucinations have distinct defining features. Which of the following statements does NOT correctly describe a characteristic of pseudohallucinations?
options: They are perceived in the outer objective space
They occur with an external stimulus
questions.explanation: In descriptive psychopathology, specifically Karl Jaspers' criteria, the defining difference between a true hallucination and a pseudohallucination is the location of the perception. True hallucinations are perceived in the outer objective space, whereas pseudohallucinations are characteristically perceived in internal subjective space (e.g., "voices in the head"). Therefore, Statement B is not accurate. Pseudohallucinations are also described as lacking the "concrete reality" or vividness (Option A) of true perceptions. Importantly, they are not voluntarily produced (Option C) and do not require an external stimulus (Option D); perceptions occurring with a stimulus are called illusions. Distinguishing these is vital; true hallucinations suggest a psychotic process (like schizophrenia), while pseudohallucinations may be seen in personality disorders or dissociative states. Recognizing that pseudohallucinations lack the quality of "external reality" helps clinicians accurately categorize a patient's perceptual disturbances and guide subsequent treatment
questions.learning: In descriptive psychopathology, specifically Karl Jaspers' criteria, the defining difference between a true hallucination and a pseudohallucination is the location of the perception.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person comes to the OPD with symptoms of not using his left side and not washing the left side of his body while bathing. On examination, he wasn't able to draw the left side of the images. Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right posterior parietal area

The given presentation and image suggest hemispatial neglect on the left side. This is likely due to a contralateral (right) parietal lobe lesion.

The right hemisphere of the brain directs attention within the entire extrapersonal space – both right and left side. If there is a lesion in the left hemisphere, there is not much contralesional neglect because the right hemisphere can compensate for both sides. The left hemisphere directs attention only in the contralateral right hemispace. If there is a lesion in the right hemisphere, it leads to severe contralesional hemineglect because the left hemisphere does not contain ipsilateral attention functions.

Patients with neglect may not be able to dress or groom the left side of the body. They may fail to copy the details on the left side of a drawing. Two bedside tests can be used to evaluate neglect:

• In simultaneous bilateral stimulation, when the examiner provides unilateral or simultaneous bilateral stimulation in the visual, auditory, or tactile modalities, patients have no difficulty detecting unilateral stimuli on either side but perceive the bilaterally presented stimulus as coming only from one side. This phenomenon is known as extinction.
• In visual target cancellation, the patient fails to detect the targets on one-half of the field in target-detection tasks.

Other features of non-dominant pareital lobe lesions include:

• Constructional apraxia
• Visuo-spatial disorientation
• Dressing apraxia
questions.learning: Right posterior parietal area — The given presentation and image suggest hemispatial neglect on the left side. This is likely due to a contralateral (right) parietal lobe lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Meiosis occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adult ovary

Meiosis occurs in the adult ovary.

Meiosis takes place only in germ cells and results in the formation of haploid gametes. Meiosis requires two cell divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II, to reduce the number of chromosomes to the haploid number of 23.

Option C: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty. Primordial germ cells (PGCs) remain dormant in the testis until puberty. At puberty, PGCs differentiate into spermatogonial stem cells. These spermatogonial stem cells then give rise to spermatogonia which marks the beginning of spermatogenesis.

Options A and D: These are somatic cells that only undergo mitosis and not meiosis.
questions.learning: Adult ovary Meiosis occurs in the adult ovary. Meiosis takes place only in germ cells and results in the formation of haploid gametes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A school bus full of children met with an accident. As the doctor in charge of triage, which of the following will you attend to first?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Airway Obstruction

The patient with airway obstruction, categorized as red, should be attended to first.

Triage is used to classify the priority of treatment. It is carried out at the site of the disaster to determine the priority for immediate medical attention, transportation, and admission to the hospital. Triage decisions are made by deciding which injuries constitute the greatest immediate threat to life. In general, airway problems are more rapidly lethal than breathing problems > circulation problems > neurologic injuries.

The internationally accepted four-color coded system is commonly used. It includes:

• Red - High-priority attention or transfer
• Yellow - Medium priority
• Green - Ambulatory patients
• Black - Dead or moribund patients
questions.learning: Airway Obstruction — The patient with airway obstruction, categorized as red, should be attended to first. Triage is used to classify the priority of treatment.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident sustains fractures of both the tibia and fibula. What type of fracture is this classified as?
questions.explanation: A "Bumper Fracture" is a clinical term for a fracture of the proximal tibia and/or fibula, typically caused by a direct blow from a car bumper to a pedestrian's leg. These are often high-energy injuries resulting in comminuted or displaced fractures of both bones at the level of the impact. Patella sleeve fractures (Option B) are specific to the pediatric population and involve an avulsion of the patellar cartilage with a small bone fragment. Depressed skull fractures (Option C) and cervical fractures (Option D) involve the cranium and spine, respectively, and are not descriptive of the leg injuries mentioned. Bumper fractures are significant because they are often associated with soft tissue damage, compartment syndrome, and injuries to the peroneal nerve or popliteal artery. Diagnosis is confirmed with X-rays showing the fracture site. Management depends on the degree of displacement and stability, often requiring surgical fixation
questions.learning: A "Bumper Fracture" is a clinical term for a fracture of the proximal tibia and/or fibula, typically caused by a direct blow from a car bumper to a pedestrian's leg.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What embryological defect is responsible for the developmental abnormalities shown in the given image?
options: Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of posterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of complete neural tube
Failure in closure of caudal neuropore of neural tube
questions.explanation: The provided image illustrates anencephaly, a lethal neural tube defect characterized by the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp. This condition results from the failure of the anterior (cranial) neuropore to close during the fourth week of embryological development, typically around day 25. When this closure fails, the developing forebrain is exposed to amniotic fluid and subsequently degenerates. Failure of the posterior or caudal neuropore (Option B and D) results in various forms of spina bifida, which affect the spinal column rather than the cranium. Complete failure of neural tube closure (Option C) leads to craniorachischisis, where both the brain and the entire spinal cord are exposed. Anencephaly is frequently associated with maternal folic acid deficiency and can be detected prenatally through elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels. Because the defect is specifically localized to the cranial vault, the anterior neuropore failure is the definitive cause
questions.learning: The provided image illustrates anencephaly, a lethal neural tube defect characterized by the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The average life expectancy for a woman in Japan is 87 years. Due to recent advances in testing for cervical cancer, there is an increase in life expectancy by 15 years. The healthcare utility value is 0.8. Which of the following can be calculated from the parameters given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. QALY

QALY (quality-adjusted life year) can be calculated by the utility value.

QALY is a disability rate indicator. It is based on the number of years that would be added to life due to medical intervention. A utility value of 1.0 is given for each year of perfect health and 0 for death. It is the measure of the disease burden which includes both quality and quantity of life.

Disability rates that are related to illness and injury are used as supplementation to mortality and morbidity indicators. It is based on the concept that a full range of daily activities implies good health. It is divided into:

• Event-type indicators: It counts the number of days of restricted activity, bed disability days, and work loss days.
• Person-type indicators: It counts limitation of mobility and limitation of activity.

Other options:

Option A: HALE (health adjusted life expectancy) is an indicator that estimates the number of years a newborn is expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality. HALE is calculated using the life expectancy at birth with an adjustment for time spent in poor health. It was known as DALE (disability-adjusted life expectancy) previously.

Option B: DALY (disability adjusted life years) is an indicator that estimates the number of years lost due to ill-health, disability, or early death. It is calculated by:

DALY= Years of life lost (YLL) + Years lived with disability (YLD)

Option C: DFLE (disability-free life expectancy) is an indicator that estimates the average number of years an individual is expected to live free of disability if the current pattern of mortality and disability continues to apply. It is also known as active life expectancy and is calculated by:

DFLE = Life expectancy - Duration of disability
questions.learning: QALY QALY (quality-adjusted life year) can be calculated by the utility value. QALY is a disability rate indicator.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man experiences sudden vision loss in his left eye for the past two hours, occurring after his retirement party. Fundoscopic examination shows the findings depicted in the image. What is the most likely cause of his acute vision loss?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of sudden, painless loss of vision in an older male and the pathognomonic fundoscopic finding of a "cherry-red spot" on a milky-white retina is diagnostic of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO). The white appearance is caused by retinal edema and ischemia; the fovea appears red because it is the thinnest part of the retina, allowing the underlying vascular choroid to show through. BRAO (Option A) would show a localized area of white edema rather than global retinal pallor. BRVO (Option B) and CRVO (Option D, "blood and thunder" fundus) present with widespread retinal hemorrhages and tortuous veins, which are completely absent here. CRAO is a medical emergency often compared to an "eye stroke," and the history of a party suggests potential triggers like hypertension or carotid emboli. Therefore, based on the classic visual triad of pallor, thin arteries, and the red spot, CRAO is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of sudden, painless loss of vision in an older male and the pathognomonic fundoscopic finding of a "cherry-red spot" on a milky-white retina is diagnostic of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The vertical fracture of the nasal septum is known as _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chevallet fracture

A Chevallet fracture usually results from a blow to the nose from below. This fracture line runs vertically. It extends from the anterior nasal spine upwards to the junction of the bony and cartilaginous dorsum of the nose.

Injuries to the nasal septum can result from trauma to the nose from the front, side, or below. The septum may get buckled on itself, fracture vertically and horizontally, or get crushed

A Jarjaway fracture (option D) results from a blow to the nose from the front. The fracture line runs horizontally backward. It begins just above the anterior nasal spine and extends just above the junction of septal cartilage with the vomer.

Early recognition and treatment of septal injuries are crucial, including drainage of hematomas.

Dislocated or fractured septal fragments should be repositioned and supported between mucoperichondrial flaps using mattress sutures and nasal packing. Nasal pyramid fractures often coincide with septal fractures and should be treated simultaneously.

Neglecting injuries to the septum can lead to deviations in the cartilaginous nose, as well as asymmetry in the nasal tip, columella, or nostrils.

Other options:

Option B: Citelli fracture is a term that does not exist. Citelli's abscess is an extratemporal complication of otitis media, occurring behind the mastoid, more towards the occipital bone. Citelli's angle refers to the sino-dural angle between the sigmoid sinus and middle cranial fossa dural plate. It is an important landmark in mastoidectomy.

Option C: A tripod fracture refers to a fracture of the zygomatic complex. There are three commonly occurring disruptions - frontozygomatic, infraorbital rim and the zygomaticomaxillary buttress.
questions.learning: Chevallet fracture — A Chevallet fracture usually results from a blow to the nose from below. This fracture line runs vertically.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant presents to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, accompanied by chest indrawing and nasal flaring, with no other significant clinical findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Under WHO IMNCI guidelines, for an infant aged 2–12 months, a respiratory rate of ≥50 breaths per minute qualifies as fast breathing (tachypnea). This patient, at 4 months old with a rate of 66, clearly meets the criteria for pneumonia. While chest indrawing and nasal flaring are present, the absence of "general danger signs"—such as inability to feed, lethargy, cyanosis, or convulsions—means the condition does not yet qualify as severe pneumonia (Option B). Severe asthma (Option C) is rarely diagnosed in infants this young and typically involves recurrent wheezing rather than isolated acute tachypnea. A common cold (Option D) would not present with significant respiratory distress or a respiratory rate this high. Standard treatment for non-severe pneumonia involves administering oral dispersible Amoxicillin and home-based care with a 5-day follow-up
questions.learning: Under WHO IMNCI guidelines, for an infant aged 2–12 months, a respiratory rate of ≥50 breaths per minute qualifies as fast breathing (tachypnea). This patient, at 4 months old with a rate of 66, clearly meets the criteria for pneumonia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old P2L2 woman presents with cervical elongation. Her family is complete. What is the preferred surgery advised?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fothergill repair

For cervical elongation in women with completed family, the preferred procedure is Fothergill (Manchester repair). Sling procedures are fertility-preserving; Le Fort is for very elderly non-sexually active women.

Cervical amputation

↓

Shortening of elongated cervix

↓

Reattachment of cardinal (Mackenrodt) ligaments

↓

Restoration of uterine support

Fothergill repair is the operation of choice for cervical elongation.

B) McCall Culdoplasty is a surgical technique used during vaginal or laparoscopic hysterectomy to prevent or treat vault prolapse or enterocele.

C) Le Fort procedure: Done for elderly women who do not desire intercourse.

D) Shirodkar sling: Used mainly for uterine prolapse, not isolated cervical elongation.
questions.learning: Fothergill repair For cervical elongation in women with completed family, the preferred procedure is Fothergill (Manchester repair). Sling procedures are fertility-preserving; Le Fort is for very elderly non-sexually active women.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 8 weeks diagnosed to have hyperthyroidism. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Propylthiouracil

PTU is preferred in the 1st trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are linked to congenital anomalies (e.g., aplasia cutis). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated. After 1st trimester, therapy is usually switched to methimazole. This switch reduces PTU-related hepatotoxicity later in pregnancy.
questions.learning: Propylthiouracil PTU is preferred in the 1st trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are linked to congenital anomalies (e.g., aplasia cutis). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: As seen in the abdominal x-ray provided, what would be the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The pelvic X-ray displays a large, well-defined, radiopaque cylindrical object (resembling a glass bottle or canister) located within the midline of the lower pelvis. The size, shape, and position are definitively diagnostic of a rectal foreign body (Option C). A ureterocele (Option B) is a small cystic dilation of the ureter and is not radio-opaque like this. A pelvic bone fracture (Option B) would show disruption of the pelvic ring architecture. A bladder stone (Option D) would typically appear as an oval, laminated, or spiculated opacity and would not have this large cylindrical "man-made" appearance. Rectal foreign bodies are usually inserted through the anus and may require surgical extraction if they cannot be retrieved manually or via endoscopy. They pose a significant risk of rectal perforation or obstruction. Therefore, based on the clear radiographic evidence of an exogenous object in the rectal vault, this is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The pelvic X-ray displays a large, well-defined, radiopaque cylindrical object (resembling a glass bottle or canister) located within the midline of the lower pelvis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
A pregnant female comes to a gynaecologist, who sends her for USG. On USG, twin pregnancy was noted with about a one-month difference in the age of fetuses. Which of the following is true with regard to this patient?

USG- Ultrasonogram
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superfetation

The above phenomenon is known as superfetation. It occurs when there is fertilization of 2 different ova released in different menstrual cycles. The consequence is two children are born at the same time and one of them might be mature while another might be immature or two fully developed fetuses are born at intervals ranging from one to three months apart.

Ovulation usually stops with the onset of pregnancy, but in a few individuals, ovulation may be possible till the first trimester, after which the decidual cavity is obliterated. The fertilization of the newly released ovum in a woman who is already pregnant may take place following coitus.

Other options:

Option A: Superfecundation is the fertilization of 2 different ova in the same menstrual cycle by separate acts of coitus. Heteropaternal superfecundation is used to refer to instances of two different males fathering fraternal twins. This leads to the possibility of twins also being half-siblings. This may raise doubts regarding adultery and infidelity.

Option C: A supposititious child is also known as a fictitious child. In such cases, a woman pretends to be pregnant and substitutes a living child as her own, or may substitute a male child for her female child, or abortion. This is done to claim property. This can be identified by verifying the signs of pregnancy and delivery in the woman and by DNA fingerprinting.

Option D: A posthumous child is a child born alive after the death of his or her father who was conceived before the death of the father.
questions.learning: Superfetation — The above phenomenon is known as superfetation. It occurs when there is fertilization of 2 different ova released in different menstrual cycles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the denominator used in calculating the incidence rate?
options: Total population at risk in a year
Total new cases in a year
questions.explanation: The Incidence Rate is a measure of the frequency with which a new disease occurs in a population over a specific period. It is calculated as the number of new cases divided by the total population at risk during that period. The "population at risk" (Option B) excludes individuals who already have the disease or are immune. The "total observed population" (Option A) is often used for prevalence rather than incidence. "Total live births" (Option C) is the denominator for fertility or neonatal mortality rates. "Total new cases" (Option D) is the numerator for the incidence calculation. Incidence reflects the rate of disease transmission and is particularly useful for studying acute conditions. It provides insights into the effectiveness of preventive interventions. For chronic diseases, incidence is often difficult to measure, and prevalence is more commonly reported. Understanding the correct denominators for various epidemiological rates is fundamental for interpreting health data and designing public health studies
questions.learning: The Incidence Rate is a measure of the frequency with which a new disease occurs in a population over a specific period. It is calculated as the number of new cases divided by the total population at risk during that period.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy presents to the outpatient department with right testicular pain following a blow from a cricket ball two hours earlier. Examination reveals severe testicular tenderness and absence of the cremasteric reflex. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of sudden, severe testicular pain following trauma, combined with an absent cremasteric reflex, are highly suggestive of testicular torsion. While trauma is the inciting event, the clinical signs point toward vascular compromise of the spermatic cord. Current guidelines recommend an urgent USG Arterial Doppler as the first diagnostic step to assess blood flow. An absence of arterial flow confirms torsion and necessitates immediate surgery. NSAIDs (Option B) only provide symptomatic relief and would dangerously delay the diagnosis of a surgical emergency. Venous Doppler (Option C) is less reliable for confirming the arterial ischemia that defines torsion. Although surgical exploration (Option D) is the definitive treatment, the trauma history lowers the pre-test probability slightly, making Doppler the preferred initial confirmatory investigation. Timely detorsion within the 6-hour "golden period" is essential to ensure testicular salvage
questions.learning: The clinical findings of sudden, severe testicular pain following trauma, combined with an absent cremasteric reflex, are highly suggestive of testicular torsion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient was involved in a road traffic accident. He was initially conscious, but later became unconscious and subsequently died. On postmortem examination, multiple petechial hemorrhages are observed in the corpus callosum. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse axonal injury

Diffuse axonal injury from rotational trauma presents with characteristic petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum, grey-white matter junctions, and brainstem, with clinical deterioration after initial consciousness.

Key Imaging Clues:

• Multiple small hemorrhagic foci
• Best seen on:

• MRI (GRE / SWI) → blooming lesions

• CT may be:

• Normal or subtle early

| Feature | DAI | Subdural Hematoma | Ischemic Injury

| ------- | --- | ----------------- | ---------------

| Mechanism | Shearing | Venous bleed | Vascular occlusion

| Location | Deep (CC, brainstem) | Extra-axial | Arterial territory

| Imaging | Tiny hemorrhages | Crescent collection | Hypodensity

| CT early | Often normal | Visible | Visible

| Best modality | MRI (GRE/SWI) | CT | MRI (DWI)
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury Diffuse axonal injury from rotational trauma presents with characteristic petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum, grey-white matter junctions, and brainstem, with clinical deterioration after initial consciousness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in renal auto-regulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal sympathetic system fibres

Renal sympathetic system fibres is not involved in the autoregulation of renal blood flow, because a denervated kidney also maintains the auto regulation of renal blood flow as that of a normal kidney.

Tubulo glomerular feedback, myogenic reflex, and renin-angiotensin system are all involved in the autoregulation of renal blood flow.

Tubulo glomerular feedback:

• When the renal artery pressure increases, the renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) increases
• This increased GFR results in increased delivery of solute and water to the early distal tubule, particularly the macula densa
• The macula dense, then secretes a vasoactive substance that constricts afferent arteriole via a paracrine mechanism
• This vasoconstriction then reduces renal blood flow and GFR back to normal

Myogenic reflex:

• The increase in renal arterial pressure stretches the walls of the afferent arterioles, which then contracts
• This contraction increases the afferent arteriolar resistance
• This increase in resistance then compensates for the increase in blood pressure, thereby keeping the renal blood flow constant.

Renin-angiotensin system:

• Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor of both afferent and efferent arterioles
• However efferent arterioles are more sensitive to angiotensin II than afferent arteriole
• Thus low levels of angiotensin II produce an increase in GFR by constricting efferent arterioles
• High levels of angiotensin II decreases GFR by constricting afferent and efferent arterioles, thereby decreasing the renal blood flow
questions.learning: Renal sympathetic system fibres Renal sympathetic system fibres is not involved in the autoregulation of renal blood flow, because a denervated kidney also maintains the auto regulation of renal blood flow as that of a normal kidney.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A chronic tobacco chewer presented with an ulcerative-nodular lesion of 4x5 cm over the lip, as shown below. Which investigation would most likely confirm his diagnosis?
options: Superficial incisional biopsy along with normal tissue
Deep incisional biopsy of Ulcer along with normal tissue
Excisional biopsy along with normal tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deep incisional biopsy of Ulcer along with normal tissue

The given clinical scenario along with the image showing ulcero-proliferative mass is suggestive of lip cancer which is a type of oral carcinoma. Histopathological diagnosis in the form of a deep incisional biopsy of an ulcer along with normal tissue is the gold standard for diagnosis.

Incisional biopsy is taken from the edge of the ulcer along with normal tissue as the centre of the ulcer is usually necrotic. A narrow deep biopsy is better than a shallow broad biopsy. (Option A)

Excisional biopsy is done for smaller benign lesions. It is not done in oral cancers as they are usually bigger in size. An excisional biopsy may increase the spread of cancer or cause functional impairment. (Option C)

Techniques like brush biopsy and exfoliative biopsy are less sensitive. Hence, they are not used for diagnosis. (Option D)
questions.learning: Deep incisional biopsy of Ulcer along with normal tissue The given clinical scenario along with the image showing ulcero-proliferative mass is suggestive of lip cancer which is a type of oral carcinoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the site of lesion in Wernicke's hemianopic pupil?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Optic tract

The site of lesion in Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is optic tract.

Wernicke hemianopic pupil is the light reflex, where, illumination of the blind half of the retina shows no pupillary reaction while stimulating the normal side of the retina shows a pupillary reaction. It is seen in lesions involving the optic tract. It is also seen in cases such as TB, syphilis and tumours of the optic thalamus.

Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.
questions.learning: Optic tract — The site of lesion in Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is optic tract. Wernicke hemianopic pupil is the light reflex, where, illumination of the blind half of the retina shows no pupillary reaction while stimulating the normal side of the retina…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following atypical antipsychotics has the highest risk of galactorrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Risperidone

Among atypical antipsychotics, risperidone and paliperidone have the highest risk of galactorrhea.

The adverse effect occurs due to their higher D2 blocking potency.
questions.learning: Risperidone Among atypical antipsychotics, risperidone and paliperidone have the highest risk of galactorrhea. The adverse effect occurs due to their higher D2 blocking potency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 29-year-old lady presents with a history of discharge from the nipple of the left breast since 1 month duration. Which one of the following is not warranted in the initial assessment of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histo/Cytopathology

A 29-year-old woman with nipple discharge requires an initial clinical and imaging assessment to identify an underlying breast lesion.

1. Clinical examination — Correct

• Assess the breast and nipple for a palpable mass, skin/nipple changes, and characteristics of the discharge.

2. Histo/Cytopathology — Incorrect / Not routinely warranted initially

• Routine cytological examination of nipple discharge has limited diagnostic value and is not part of the standard initial evaluation.
• Tissue diagnosis is performed when imaging or examination identifies a suspicious lesion.

3. Mammography — Correct

• May be performed when clinically indicated, particularly when the discharge is pathological or there are suspicious findings.

4. Ultrasonography — Correct

• Ultrasound is particularly useful in women <30 years and is generally the preferred initial imaging modality for a breast abnormality in this age group.
questions.learning: Histo/Cytopathology — A 29-year-old woman with nipple discharge requires an initial clinical and imaging assessment to identify an underlying breast lesion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A soldier presents 24 hours after a high-velocity shrapnel injury to the right thigh with severe pain and crepitus at the wound site. Which microorganism is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a high-velocity shrapnel injury followed by severe discomfort and crepitus (gas in the tissues) within 24 hours is pathognomonic for Gas Gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis). The primary causative agent in approximately 80-95% of cases is Clostridium perfringens. This anaerobic, gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus thrives in the devitalized, ischemic environment created by trauma, producing potent toxins like alpha-toxin that lead to rapid tissue necrosis and gas production . While Clostridium septicum (Option A) and Clostridium novyi (Option C) can also cause gas gangrene, they are significantly less common than C. perfringens in traumatic settings. Clostridium difficile (Option B) is responsible for antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis and does not cause soft tissue infections like myonecrosis. Management of gas gangrene is a surgical emergency involving aggressive debridement of all necrotic tissue, high-dose intravenous antibiotics (penicillin and clindamycin), and sometimes hyperbaric oxygen therapy. The presence of crepitus is a critical clinical sign that necessitates immediate intervention to prevent systemic toxemia, multi-organ failure, and death
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a high-velocity shrapnel injury followed by severe discomfort and crepitus (gas in the tissues) within 24 hours is pathognomonic for Gas Gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions does not form a grey-white membrane over the tonsils ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ludwig’s angina

Ludwig’s angina does not cause a grey-white membrane over the tonsils. It is the submandibular space infection.

D/D for membrane over tonsil:

* Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms

* Diphtheria

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Vincent’s angina

* Leukemia

* Candida

* Agranulocytosis

* Malignancy

* Aphthous ulcer

* Traumatic ulcer

Ludwig’s Angina is the infection of submandibular space.

One side of the submandibular space is the superficial layer of deep cervical fascia that extends between the hyoid bone and the mandible, while the other side is the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth and the tongue. The mylohyoid muscle separates it into two compartments:

* Sublingual compartment (above the mylohyoid).

* Submaxillary and submental compartments (below the mylohyoid).

Both compartments freely communicate in the midline with the opposite side. Therefore, infection rapidly becomes bilateral.

Dental infections are the most common cause and account for 80% of the cases.

Clinical features:

* Marked difficulty in swallowing (odynophagia) with varying degrees of trismus.

* When infection is localized to the sublingual space, structures in the floor of the mouth are swollen and tongue seems to be pushed up and back.

* When the infection spreads to the submaxillary space, submental and submandibular regions become swollen, tender and impart woody-hard feel.

* Usually, there is cellulitis of the tissues rather than frank abscess.

* The tongue is progressively pushed upwards and backward threatening the airway.

Treatment:

* Systemic antibiotics.

* Incision and drainage of an abscess.

* Tracheostomy, if there is severe obstruction of the airway.
questions.learning: Ludwig’s angina Ludwig’s angina does not cause a grey-white membrane over the tonsils. It is the submandibular space infection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was rushed to the emergency department after being hit in the head in a road traffic accident The patient was unconscious. CT-scan revealed an extradural hematoma. Which of the following is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pterion

The pterion is most likely to be injured. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

Pterion is an H shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

* Frontal bone

* Squamous part of the temporal bone

* Greater wing of sphenoid bone

* Parietal bone.

It is an important structure as it overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.
questions.learning: Pterion — The pterion is most likely to be injured. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following type of renal calculi is resistant to the extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystine

Cystine stones are resistant to extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) due to their hardness. Cystine, brushite, and calcium oxalate monohydrate stones are the most refractory to ESWL fragmentation, with cystine and brushite being the most resistant.

ESWL is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body that focus on the stones. It is the most common method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 1.5 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.

Complications: Infection, haematuria, parenchymal hemorrhage, and perirenal hematoma.

Contraindications: Obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants.

Note: Stone fragments collecting in the distal ureter following ESWL are known as steinstrasse.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient with chronic sinusitis and persistent nasal congestion is being evaluated with a focus on the anatomical pathways responsible for sinus drainage, particularly the bulla ethmoidalis. Which anatomical structure serves as the primary drainage pathway for the bulla ethmoidalis?
questions.explanation: The bulla ethmoidalis is the largest of the anterior ethmoid air cells and a key landmark in endoscopic sinus surgery. It drains directly into the Middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall. Specifically, it typically opens into the hiatus semilunaris or just superior to it. The Superior meatus (Option B) receives the posterior ethmoid cells and the sphenoid sinus (via the sphenoethmoidal recess). The Inferior meatus (Option C) only receives the nasolacrimal duct. The Middle concha (Option D) is the bony turbinate structure that covers the middle meatus but is not a drainage pathway itself. Understanding these drainage patterns is critical for managing chronic sinusitis. Obstruction within the middle meatus (the osteomeatal complex) can lead to the simultaneous involvement of the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. Successful sinus surgery aims to restore the natural drainage pathways through these specific meatuses. The bulla ethmoidalis is often the first structure removed during an ethmoidectomy to gain access to the posterior cells
questions.learning: The bulla ethmoidalis is the largest of the anterior ethmoid air cells and a key landmark in endoscopic sinus surgery. It drains directly into the Middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presented with fever and massive splenomegaly. On palpation, the spleen was 15 cm and directed obliquely when measured from the right iliac fossa. Which of the following structures prevent the vertical and downward descent of the spleen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phrenicocolic ligament

The vertical and downward descent of the spleen is prevented by the phrenicocolic ligament.

The phrenicocolic ligament is not attached to the spleen. It attaches the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm.

When the spleen gets enlarged, the phrenicocolic ligament along with the splenic flexure of the colon restricts its downward displacement. The enlargement of the spleen occurs towards the right iliac fossa and hence the spleen is directed obliquely.
Splenic ligaments and their attachments:

Splenic ligament
Attachments

The spleen becomes palpable when it is enlarged 2-3 times more than its normal size. A characteristic splenic notch can be felt in the medial border in an enlarged spleen. Also, fingers cannot be insinuated between the left costal margin and the enlarged spleen.

In the classical method of palpation, the right hand (with fingers pointed towards the left costal margin) is placed on the right iliac fossa. Palpation begins from the right iliac fossa towards the left hypochondrium in an upwards and lateral direction. Between each breath of the patient, the edge of the spleen can be felt.

In the hooking method, the hooked fingers of the right hand are placed under the left costal margin, and with the left hand, pressure is exerted over the posterolateral aspect of the lower thorax. Spleen is felt at the deep inspiratory phase.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The graph below depicts the dose response with multiple administrations of the drug. Which of the following statements is false regarding the phenomenon shown in this graph
options: Drugs are given at short intervals in the same dose
Drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses
This incident is seen with drugs such as ephedrine
This action is rarely seen in clinical practice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses

The graph below shows a rapidly diminishing response to repeated administration, a phenomenon known as tachyphylaxis. The false statement regarding tachyphylaxis is drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses.

The term tachyphylaxis is used to describe desensitization that occurs very rapidly, sometimes with the initial dose. Continued stimulation results in a state of desensitization thus the effect of continued or repeated exposure to the same concentration of a drug is diminished.

This phenomenon is usually demonstrated in the experimental setup depicted by indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as ephedrine, amphetamine, and tyrosine. Repeated administration in the same dose usually leads to the uptake of drugs and exhaustion of neurotransmitters. Hence tachyphylaxis is a rapid development.

However, tolerance encountered in the clinical setting is developed slowly. The original effect of the drug can be recovered by increasing the dose in case of tolerance. However, it is not possible in the case of tachyphylaxis due to the exhaustion of mediators or due to the fast desensitization of the target cell.
questions.learning: Drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses The graph below shows a rapidly diminishing response to repeated administration, a phenomenon known as tachyphylaxis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with perioral numbness, tingling, and tetany. All the following conditions can lead to this, except _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin D toxicity

The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with perioral paresthesias and tetany is suggestive of hypocalcemia. Vitamin D toxicity does not cause hypocalcemia but rather leads to hypercalcemia.

Vitamin D toxicity occurs due to excessive intake of vitamin D supplements, usually in amounts of >40,000–100,000 IU/day. The symptoms are mainly due to hypercalcemia. Laboratory investigations will show elevated serum vitamin-D levels (>100 ng/mL) and calcium.

In such patients, vitamin D supplements should be discontinued immediately, along with restricted exposure to the sun and avoiding calcium supplements. Since vitamin D is stored in the body for a long time, the symptoms may persist for some days even after stopping the intake.

Causes of hypocalcemia

• Pancreatitis (sequestration of the calcium via chelation with free fatty acids)
• Renal failure/chronic kidney disease (impaired 1,25(OH)2D production)
• Pancreatic and small bowel fistulas
• Hypoparathyroidism (PTH is the main defense against hypocalcemia)
• Abnormalities in magnesium levels
• Tumor lysis syndrome

Symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia may be circumoral or digital numbness, paresthesia, laryngeal spasms, and cardiac arrhythmias. Given below are two named signs of hypocalcemia.

• Chvostek sign: This is elicited by gently tapping over the facial nerve in front of the tragus of the ear. There is hyperexcitability of the facial muscles, manifesting as a contraction of the muscles.
• Trousseau sign: This is elicited by making the forearm ischemic by applying a sphygmomanometer cuff to the arm and keeping the pressure above systolic blood pressure (SBP) for 5 minutes. The hand goes into a painful carpopedal spasm and assumes the accoucheur’s hand position (shown in the image below).

The below image shows Trousseau's sign:

Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is an emergency and must be treated with:

• 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate is given slowly through the intravenous route.
• Calcium and vitamin D replacement is given orally.
• Magnesium supplementation may also be required due to the synergistic actions of calcium and magnesium.

Calcitonin and bisphosphonates are used in cases of severe toxicity causing hypercalcemia. Some patients might require glucocorticoids, which lower plasma calcium levels by reducing calcium absorption from the intestines and increasing its urinary excretion.
questions.learning: Vitamin D toxicity — The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with perioral paresthesias and tetany is suggestive of hypocalcemia. Vitamin D toxicity does not cause hypocalcemia but rather leads to hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The following parameter in ALL indicate a poor prognosis ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Age >10 years

Age >10 years indicates a poor prognosis in ALL.

Leukocyte count <50,000/mm3, hyperdiploidy, and trisomy of chromosomes 4,10,17 indicate a good prognosis.
questions.learning: Age >10 years Age >10 years indicates a poor prognosis in ALL. Leukocyte count <50,000/mm3, hyperdiploidy, and trisomy of chromosomes 4,10,17 indicate a good prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During a routine examination, a young asymptomatic male is found to have a wide, fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) on auscultation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A wide, fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) is the pathognomonic physical finding for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option A). Normally, S2 splits slightly during inspiration. In ASD, the continuous left-to-right shunt increases right ventricular volume throughout the entire respiratory cycle, causing the pulmonic valve to close consistently later than the aortic valve, regardless of breathing. VSD (Option B) typically presents with a pansystolic murmur. Tetralogy of Fallot (Option C) presents with cyanosis and a single S2. Bicuspid Aortic Valve (Option D) is characterized by an early systolic click. Because the finding of a "fixed split" is so uniquely specific to the physiology of an interatrial shunt, ASD is the definitive clinical diagnosis. Most young patients are asymptomatic initially, which is why this auscultatory finding is often discovered during routine screening. Management may involve percutaneous or surgical closure
questions.learning: A wide, fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) is the pathognomonic physical finding for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option A). Normally, S2 splits slightly during inspiration.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Y chromosome

The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the presence or absence of the Y chromosome as follows:

• In presence of the Y chromosome, the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) produces the protein called the testis determining factor which leads to the gonads developing as the testes. The Sertoli cells of the testis will then produce a peptide hormone, the Müllerian inhibiting substance (MIS), also known as Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and cause the Müllerian ducts to regress.
• In absence of the Y chromosome and the SRY gene consequently, the gonads will develop as ovaries and the Mullerian duct will differentiate into the fallopian tubes and the upper part of the vagina. The WNT4 gene on the 1st chromosome promotes female sex development.
questions.learning: Y chromosome — The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the presence or absence of the Y chromosome as follows: • In presence of the Y chromosome, the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) produces the protein called the testis…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true with respect to the Little's area?
options: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.
It is situated at the postero-inferior part of the nasal septum.
Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

The correct statement among the following is Option A, Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

Little's area:

Little’s area, situated at the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum is the most common site of epistaxis in children and young adults. 90% of bleeds arise from Little's area, where the Kiesselbach plexus is situated on the nasal septum.

Factors that increase the risk of epistaxis in children when compared to adults, include the habit of nose picking and increased friability of mucosa due to frequent upper respiratory tract infections.

Kiesselbach’s plexus:

Four arteries anastomose at the anterior inferior part of the nasal septum (Little's area) to form a vascular plexus called Kiesselbach’s plexus.

* Anterior ethmoidal

* Septal branch of the superior labial

* Septal branch of sphenopalatine

* Septal branch of the greater palatine
questions.learning: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area. The correct statement among the following is Option A, Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Confusion assessment test is used in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delirium

Confusion assessment test is used in detection of delirium.

Delirium is reported to occur in a wide range of mechanically ventilated ICU patients and can be detected by the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)-ICU or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist. These tools are used to ask patients to answer simple questions and perform simple tasks and can be used readily at the bedside.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of the enzyme tyrosine transaminase leads to the development of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Type II Tyrosinemia (also known as Richner-Hanhart syndrome) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme tyrosine transaminase (also called tyrosine aminotransferase). This enzyme catalyzes the first step of tyrosine breakdown. Its deficiency leads to elevated levels of tyrosine in the blood and tissues, characteristically presenting with painful corneal erosions (pseudodendritic keratitis) and hyperkeratotic lesions on the palms and soles. Type I Tyrosinemia (Option A) is caused by a deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase and is the most severe form, often leading to liver failure. Alkaptonuria (Option C) results from a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase, causing dark urine and ochronosis. Type III Tyrosinemia (Option D) is rare and caused by a deficiency of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase. Understanding these specific enzymatic defects in the tyrosine catabolic pathway is essential for diagnosing inborn errors of metabolism and initiating targeted dietary management to prevent systemic and ocular complications
questions.learning: Type II Tyrosinemia (also known as Richner-Hanhart syndrome) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme tyrosine transaminase (also called tyrosine aminotransferase).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the level of lymph nodes indicated in the marked region of the neck in the given anatomical image.
questions.explanation: The marked lymph nodes are located along the upper part of the internal jugular vein, extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, which corresponds to Level II (Upper Jugular Nodes). This level includes the clinically significant jugulodigastric node, which is frequently involved in malignancies of the oropharynx and nasopharynx. Regarding the distractors, Level Ia (Option B) refers to submental nodes in the midline under the chin, and Level Ib (Option C) refers to submandibular nodes lateral to them. Level IV (Option D) consists of lower jugular nodes located between the cricoid cartilage and the clavicle. The vertical position of the nodes along the superior third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle as shown in the image confirms they belong to Level II. Identifying these levels is crucial for staging and planning neck dissections in head and neck cancer patients
questions.learning: The marked lymph nodes are located along the upper part of the internal jugular vein, extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, which corresponds to Level II (Upper Jugular Nodes).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of penetrating injury to the eye. A diagnosis of sympathetic ophthalmitis was confirmed. Which of the following will be seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Panuveitis

Panuveitis is the usual clinical manifestation seen in sympathetic ophthalmitis. Panuveitis is inflammation of the whole uvea.

Sympathetic ophthalmitis is a granulomatous pan-uveitis that usually occurs after penetrative trauma. It can also develop after intraocular surgery. Both the injured eye (exciting eye) and fellow eye (sympathizing eye) develop panuveitis. Trauma to the ciliary region (dangerous zone) poses an increased risk.

It is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction. According to the allergic theory, the uveal pigment in the injured eye acts as an allergen that causes uveitis in the other eye. Dalen-Fuchs nodules (proliferation of pigment epithelium), exudative retinal detachment, and optic disc swelling can be seen on fundoscopy. A sunset glow appearance can persist due to residual chorioretinal scarring.

Dalen-Fuchs nodules are depicted in the image below.

The exciting eye shows features of low-grade uveitis such as ciliary congestion, lacrimation, and tenderness. The sympathizing eye is usually involved 4-8 weeks later. It has a prodromal stage with photophobia, ciliary congestion, and keratic precipitates. In the fully developed stage, symptoms of acute iridocyclitis supervene.

Prophylactic measures to be taken before the condition sets in include topical or systemic steroids and antibiotics. Early excision of the injured eye is carried out if it cannot be salvaged. Once sympathetic ophthalmitis has already set in, enucleation of the injured eye must be done. Atropine, immunosuppressants, and corticosteroids should also be administered.

Other options:

Options A and D: Anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris up to pars plicata. Keratic precipitates are characteristic of the condition. Acute anterior uveitis, which can last for 6 weeks to 3 months, presents with pain, photophobia, and lacrimation. Chronic anterior uveitis lasts for longer than 6 months. Anterior uveitis is associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, and ankylosing spondylitis.

The image below shows keratic precipitates.

Option B: Pars planitis or intermediate uveitis is an inflammatory condition that affects the pars plana of the ciliary body, the peripheral retina, the choroid, and the vitreous base. Snowbanking is the hallmark feature. It is a grey-white fibrovascular plaque formed due to the coalescence of snowball opacities over the pars plana. Pars planitis can be seen in multiple sclerosis, sarcoidosis, and syphilis.
questions.learning: Panuveitis Panuveitis is the usual clinical manifestation seen in sympathetic ophthalmitis. Panuveitis is inflammation of the whole uvea.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A chronic smoker wants to quit smoking. Which of the following drugs would help him with his goal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Both a and c

Bupropion and Varenicline are used for smoking cessation.

Bupropion:

* It enhances both noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission by inhibiting reuptake.

* Used for aiding smoking cessation and for the treatment of depression in combination with SSRIs.

* Adverse effects of bupropion include stimulant side effects like tachycardia, insomnia, headache, and seizures in anorexic/bulimic patients.

* It decreases the risk of sexual dysfunction and weight gain compared to other antidepressants.

Varenicline:

* Nicotinic ACh receptor partial agonist.

* Used for smoking cessation.

* Side effects: Sleep disturbance, may depress mood and increase suicidal tendencies.

Mirtazapine:

* Serotonin receptor antagonist.

* Used for the treatment of depression in combination with SSRIs and for insomnia in depressive patients.

* Side effect: Sedation.
questions.learning: Both a and c Bupropion and Varenicline are used for smoking cessation. Bupropion: * It enhances both noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission by inhibiting reuptake. * Used for aiding smoking cessation and for the treatment of depression in…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In the case presented, can you identify the imaging technique employed and the specific diagnosis related to the kidneys?
questions.explanation: The image displays characteristic MRI features — notably the bright white (hyperintense) rounded structures on this T2-weighted sequence. MRI uses magnetic fields, and fluid-filled cysts appear brilliantly white on T2 imaging. CT scans appear in Hounsfield grayscale with different tissue contrast, lacking this distinctive fluid brightness pattern. Diagnosis — Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD) : Both kidneys are massively enlarged, completely replaced by innumerable cysts of varying sizes, with virtually no normal renal parenchyma visible. This is the classic appearance of Autosomal Dominant PKD (ADPKD), the most common inherited kidney disorder. The bilateral symmetrical involvement with hundreds of cysts is pathognomonic. Why Other Options are Wrong: (B) CT of Polycystic Kidney Disease : The imaging modality is MRI not CT; the bright white fluid signal on T2 confirms MRI technique. (C) MRI of Horseshoe Kidney : Horseshoe kidney shows fusion of lower poles across the midline with normal parenchyma : no multiple cysts present. (D) CT of Horseshoe Kidney : Wrong both in modality (CT) and diagnosis (horseshoe); neither matches the bilateral cystic enlargement seen here
questions.learning: The image displays characteristic MRI features — notably the bright white (hyperintense) rounded structures on this T2-weighted sequence. MRI uses magnetic fields, and fluid-filled cysts appear brilliantly white on T2 imaging.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements about claudication pain is not true?
options: Rest pain is seen more in the night
Pain in intermittent claudication comes at first step of walking.
The clinical stem does not reflect the site of peripheral arterial obstruction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pain in intermittent claudication comes at first step of walking.

Pain in intermittent claudication is brought on by walking and doesnot start with the first step of walking.

Peripheral artery occlusion or stenosis is predominantly caused by atherosclerosis or atheroma (Option C) and thromboembolic disease. The resulting stenosis or occlusion produces signs and symptoms related to the organ that is supplied by the affected artery. Such occlusion in the lower limbs presents with claudication pain, rest pain, and gangrene. Though the muscle groups affected by claudication are present at one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease, the clinical stem does not reflect the exact site of the peripheral arterial obstruction. (Option D)

Intermittent claudication pain is a feature of arterial stenosis or occlusion that occurs due to the anaerobic metabolism occurring in the muscle. Claudication pain may be of different types and can be differentiated as follows:

• Vascular (intermittent) claudication pain is brought on by walking and is relieved by rest within 5 minutes. (Option B)
• Claudication pain present on taking the first step of walking is classical for osteoarthritis.
• Neurogenic claudication occurs with changes in the position of the back such as bending forward and straightening. It takes more time to be relieved by rest (more than 5 minutes). It may be seen in cases of nerve compression from lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse or spinal stenosis.

Rest pain occurs when the occlusive disease progresses in severity and anaerobic respiration occurs even at rest. Though this pain is present during the day, it is exacerbated on lying down at night (Option A) due to loss of gravity dependant perfusion of the foot. This may be relieved by hanging the foot out of the bed to restore the gravitational effects.
questions.learning: Pain in intermittent claudication comes at first step of walking. Pain in intermittent claudication is brought on by walking and doesnot start with the first step of walking.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following structures are not removed in radical neck dissection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sublingual gland

Sublingual gland is not removed in radical neck dissection (RND). Submandibular gland is removed in RND.

RND involves the removal of:

• All lymph nodes from Levels I through to V (submental, submandibular, upper, middle, and lower jugular, and posterior triangle regions) along with its fibrofatty tissue.
• The spinal accessory nerve
• Internal jugular vein
• Sternocleidomastoid muscle
• Tail of parotid
• Submandibular gland
• Omohyoid muscle
questions.learning: Sublingual gland Sublingual gland is not removed in radical neck dissection (RND). Submandibular gland is removed in RND.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Steroid hormone receptors bind to specific DNA sequences via which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc finger motif

After binding their hormone ligand, steroid hormone receptors dimerize, translocate to the nucleus (if not already nuclear), and bind to specific DNA sequences (HREs) through the zinc finger DNA-binding domain, thereby activating or repressing transcription of target genes.

Why not the other options?

• B. RNA motif: Involved in RNA binding, not DNA binding by steroid receptors.
• C. Leucine zipper: DNA-binding motif found in transcription factors such as c-Fos and c-Jun (AP-1).
• D. Helix-turn-helix: DNA-binding motif seen in homeobox proteins and many prokaryotic transcription factors, not steroid hormone receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is being assessed by palpation in the image shown below?
questions.explanation: The image shows palpation being performed posterior to the medial malleolus — the anatomical landmark for the posterior tibial artery, which runs in the groove between the medial malleolus and the calcaneus. Key Anatomical Features: 1. 1. Fingers placed behind medial malleolus 2. 2. Classic position for posterior tibial pulse assessment 3. 3. Important pulse for assessing peripheral vascular disease 4. 4. Absent in peripheral arterial occlusive disease Why other options are wrong: (A) Anterior tibial artery is incorrect because anterior tibial artery is palpated on the dorsum of the foot between first and second metatarsals : not behind the medial malleolus. (C) Dorsalis pedis artery is incorrect because dorsalis pedis is palpated on the dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon : not at the medial malleolar groove as shown. (D) Popliteal artery is incorrect because popliteal artery is palpated in the popliteal fossa behind the knee with knee slightly flexed : completely different anatomical location from what is shown here

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Following appearance in IVP is caused by ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ureterocoele

The image depicts cobra head/ adder head deformity in an IVP of bilateral ureteroceles.

* Ureterocoeles represent congenital dilatation of the distal-most portion of the ureter. The dilated portion of the ureter may herniate into the bladder secondary to the abnormal structure of vesicoureteric junction (VUJ).

* The cobra head sign (or spring onion sign) refers to dilatation of the distal ureter, surrounded by a thin lucent line, which is seen in patients with an adult-type ureterocoele. The cobra head appearance indicates an uncomplicated ureterocele.
questions.learning: Ureterocoele — The image depicts cobra head/ adder head deformity in an IVP of bilateral ureteroceles. * Ureterocoeles represent congenital dilatation of the distal-most portion of the ureter.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a known history of lung cancer presents with shortness of breath and dizziness. On physical examination, breath sounds are markedly diminished over the left lower scapular region. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a known history of lung cancer, the development of dyspnea (shortness of breath) and reduced breath sounds over a specific lung area (the left lower scapular region) is highly suggestive of a malignant pleural effusion. This occurs when cancer cells spread to the pleura, causing fluid to accumulate in the pleural space, which compresses the underlying lung and blocks sound transmission. Pneumothorax (Option D) also causes reduced breath sounds but typically presents more acutely with a sudden "pop" or sharp pain. Constrictive pericarditis (Option A) and Cardiac tamponade (Option C) would present with distant heart sounds and elevated neck veins rather than localized absent breath sounds. Diagnosis of pleural effusion is confirmed by chest X-ray showing a "meniscus sign" and blunting of the costophrenic angle. Management involves therapeutic thoracocentesis (draining the fluid) for symptom relief and cytological analysis to confirm the malignant nature of the effusion
questions.learning: In a patient with a known history of lung cancer, the development of dyspnea (shortness of breath) and reduced breath sounds over a specific lung area (the left lower scapular region) is highly suggestive of a malignant pleural effusion.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with inspiratory stridor that worsens during crying and feeding. Which statement is true regarding the most likely diagnosis?
options: Omega sign, improves in prone position
Thumb sign, improves in tripod position
Thumb sign, improves in tripod position Steeple sign is seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Omega sign, improves in prone position

Recognize laryngomalacia as the most common cause of congenital inspiratory stridor. It typically presents within the first few weeks to months of life with inspiratory stridor that worsens during crying, feeding, or when supine and improves in the prone position. Laryngoscopy shows a characteristic omega-shaped, floppy epiglottis with collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration.

Why not the other options?

• B. Thumb sign, improves in tripod position: Thumb sign indicates acute epiglottitis, which presents with high fever, drooling, dysphagia, and toxic appearance, not a chronic infantile stridor.
• C. Steeple sign is seen: Steeple sign is characteristic of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) on AP neck X-ray, presenting with barking cough and stridor.
• D. Epiglottis is reddish and oedematous: Seen in acute epiglottitis, not laryngomalacia.
questions.learning: Omega sign, improves in prone position Recognize laryngomalacia as the most common cause of congenital inspiratory stridor. It typically presents within the first few weeks to months of life with inspiratory stridor that worsens during crying, feeding, or…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In fetal alcohol syndrome, which of the following is not seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Macrocephaly

Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is associated with microcephaly rather than macrocephaly.

Alcohol exposure during pregnancy results in reduced brain volume in the frontal lobe, striatum, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and cerebellum. It also causes thinning of the corpus callosum and abnormal functioning of the amygdala.

Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASDs) are the leading preventable causes of developmental delay and intellectual disability. FASDs encompass different conditions such as FAS, partial FAS, alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder, alcohol-related birth defect, and neurobehavioral disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure.

Diagnostic criteria for FASDs include characteristic facial features, prenatal/postnatal growth deficiency, neurobehavioral impairment, and maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy.

The facial features of FAS include short palpebral fissures, a thin upper lip vermilion border, a smooth philtrum, epicanthic folds, a flattened nasal bridge, lowset and unparallel ears, and retarded midfacial development.

CNS involvement leads to microcephaly, incomplete holoprosencephaly, and agenesis of the corpus callosum and the cerebellar vermis. The neurocognitive features include developmental delays, inattention, impulsivity, social impairments, and behavioral difficulties. Common comorbidities include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), self-regulation problems, and impulse control issues. Cardiac anomalies are also seen, with VSD being more common than ASD and tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.learning: Macrocephaly Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is associated with microcephaly rather than macrocephaly. Alcohol exposure during pregnancy results in reduced brain volume in the frontal lobe, striatum, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and cerebellum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic woman with a recent history of COVID-19 treatment using steroids and remdesivir now presents with foul-smelling nasal discharge and a black necrotic lesion in the nasal cavity, with erosion of the nasal septum and hard palate. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is an opportunistic fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales. This case describes the classic clinical scenario often seen during the COVID-19 pandemic: an immunocompromised patient (due to diabetes and steroid use) developing a fulminant infection. The "black necrotic mass" (eschar) is pathognomonic and results from the fungus's angioinvasive nature, which causes tissue infarction and necrosis. Erosion of the hard palate and nasal septum indicates rapid local spread. Option A (Aspergillosis) can be invasive but rarely presents with such rapid, aggressive necrosis in this specific context. Option C (Foreign body) would cause unilateral discharge but not palatal erosion. Option D (Rhinosporidiosis) presents as strawberry-like friable nasal polyps, usually in patients with a history of bathing in stagnant water. Mucormycosis is a surgical emergency requiring aggressive debridement and systemic antifungal therapy with amphotericin B. Delay in diagnosis often leads to blindness or fatal intracranial extension

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pharmacodynamics refers to which aspect of a drug’s action or profile?
options: Mode of excretion of a drug
Mechanism of action of a drug
Transport of drug across biological membranes
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics is broadly defined as "what the drug does to the body." It encompasses the study of the mechanism of action of a drug, its biochemical and physiological effects, and the relationship between drug concentration and its effect at the site of action. This includes receptor binding, post-receptor signaling, and chemical interactions. In contrast, Pharmacokinetics is "what the body does to the drug," which includes the mode of excretion (Option A), transport across biological membranes (Option C, part of absorption and distribution), and metabolism. Latency of onset (Option D) is a clinical observation influenced by both pharmacokinetic factors (how fast it reaches the site) and pharmacodynamic factors (how fast it binds to the receptor). Understanding pharmacodynamics is essential for determining the therapeutic index, potency, and efficacy of a medication. Therefore, the mechanism of action is the core component that defines the pharmacodynamic profile of any pharmacological agent

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the anatomical structure indicated in the given image.
questions.explanation: The anatomical feature highlighted in the sagittal section is the genioglossus muscle, often referred to as the "safety muscle" of the tongue. It is a fan-shaped extrinsic muscle that arises from the superior genial tubercle of the mandible and inserts into the tongue's substance and the hyoid bone body. Its primary function is the protrusion of the tongue. Clinically, paralysis of the genioglossus allows the tongue to fall back and obstruct the airway, which is why it is vital in anesthesiology and airway management. Option B, the hyoglossus, is a quadrilateral muscle that depresses the tongue. Option C, the styloglossus, originates from the styloid process and retracts the tongue. Option D, the palatoglossus, is technically a muscle of the soft palate that elevates the tongue's posterior portion. Understanding these extrinsic muscles is essential for diagnosing hypoglossal nerve injuries, where the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side upon protrusion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 44-year-old man is referred to your center for management of severe hyperglycemia. During examination, you note that the patient has enlarged feet, coarse facial features and prognathism. You suspect acromegaly. Which of the following tests can you use as a screening method for this condition?
options: Oral glucose challenge test with GH level
Insulin-like growth factor-1 binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insulin like growth factor-1 levels

The best screening test for acromegaly is the measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) level.

Other options:

Options A and B: Oral glucose challenge test with growth hormone (GH) levels is used for further confirmation of the diagnosis. Increased insulin-like growth factor-1 binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) levels can also be seen in patients with acromegaly. But they are not typically used as initial screening methods.

Option D: IGF-1 levels are more reliable than random GH levels because GH secretion is pulsatile. IGF-1 levels reflect long-term exposure to GH and provide a more stable indicator of excessive GH production.

Acromegaly is characterized by excessive GH secretion, usually caused by a somatotrope adenoma in the pituitary gland. It can also be due to ectopic GH secretion or hypothalamic tumors.

The clinical presentation of acromegaly includes frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, coarse facial features, mandibular prognathism, widened space between lower incisors and other manifestations such as soft tissue swelling, deepening voice, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthropathy, and acanthosis nigricans.

It can also lead to cardiovascular complications (cardiomyopathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, and hypertension), obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes mellitus, an increased risk of colon polyps, and colonic malignancy.

The primary treatment for acromegaly is surgical resection of GH-secreting adenomas. Somatostatin receptor ligands like octreotide and lanreotide, which suppress GH and IGF-1 levels, are used as adjuvant treatment or when surgery is not possible or unsuccessful. Radiation therapy may be considered for patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to medical therapy. Other treatment options include GH receptor antagonists like pegvisomant and dopamine agonists like cabergoline.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with myelofibrosis has been taking ruxolitinib for the past 6 months with good symptom control. He develops oral candidiasis and is started on ketoconazole. After 3–4 days of antifungal therapy, he experiences dizziness, severe fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent episodes of hypotension. Blood investigations reveal new-onset anemia and thrombocytopenia. What is the most likely cause of these adverse effects?
options: Induction of CYP3A4 by ketoconazole leading to increased metabolism of ruxolitinib
Inhibition of CYP3A4 by ketoconazole leading to increased plasma levels of ruxolitinib
Reduced gastrointestinal absorption of ruxolitinib due to ketoconazole
Displacement of ruxolitinib from plasma protein binding sites by ketoconazole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of CYP3A4 by ketoconazole leading to increased plasma levels of ruxolitinib

Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor used in myelofibrosis, is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. Concomitant administration of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole decreases its metabolism, resulting in increased plasma concentrations and a higher risk of dose-dependent toxicities, including myelosuppression (anemia, thrombocytopenia), dizziness, fatigue, infections, and hypotension. Dose adjustment of ruxolitinib is recommended when used with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

Why not the other options?

• A. Induction of CYP3A4 by ketoconazole leading to increased metabolism of ruxolitinib: Incorrect. Ketoconazole is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor, not an inducer.
• C. Reduced gastrointestinal absorption of ruxolitinib due to ketoconazole: Incorrect. Ketoconazole does not significantly impair ruxolitinib absorption.
• D. Displacement of ruxolitinib from plasma protein binding sites by ketoconazole: Incorrect. This is not a clinically significant mechanism for the interaction between ketoconazole and ruxolitinib.
questions.learning: Inhibition of CYP3A4 by ketoconazole leading to increased plasma levels of ruxolitinib Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor used in myelofibrosis, is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4.

questions.text: Which one of the following ion is released by the ryanodine receptor (RyR) leading to malignant hyperthermia?
